In a recent development, fierce Healthcare is tracking workforce changes across healthcare in 2026. Stick with this tracker for the latest updates, and reach out to the team with any layoff news. Also, take a look back at our trackers for 2025 and 2024.

Electronic health record and software tech giant athenahealth is laying off about 4% of its total workforce, according to a Boston Globe report and subsequent LinkedIn posts from affected workers.

Recent findings suggest that CEO Bob Segert reportedly informed employees in a Nov. 13 email, in which he cited healthcare provider visits "below our expectations," an overly complex organizational structure and opportunities for AI to "rethink the work itself," according to the Globe.

The firm has not given a hard number on how many employees are affected. Its last round of layoffs in early 2023 trimmed 178 jobs, which at the time reflected less than 3% of its total workforce.

Ascension will begin laying off 51 St. Louis workers on Jan. 8, according to a Nov. 6 WARN notice filed with the Missouri Office of Workforce Development.

Sources indicate that the cuts are reportedly tied to the health system's decision to hand the administration of its employee health plan to Luminare Health, a Health Care Service Corp. subsidiary. That change takes effect Jan. 1, with the health plan for Ascension employees and their dependents changing its branding from SmartHealth to the Ascension Health Plan.

A representative of the health system told press the partners are working to offer potential retention or placement support ahead of the changeover, and that those who do not stay with either organization will receive severance.

Kootenai Health, a Northern Idaho nonprofit health system, is reportedly trimming 80 positions, or about 2% of its 4,500-plus workforce.

The system told Coeur d'Alene Press that it has been pressured by slow-to-increase Medicare reimbursement, higher expenses, commercial payment delays and the loss of statutory discounts when its primary 397-bed hospital no longer qualified as a 340B Disproportionate Share Hospital two years back. It also pointed to a rising population in its communities, driving a need for additional investments into more hospital space to meet demand.

The system did not outline what types of roles are affected, but remarked it still at the moment has 139 other positions that are open.

Healthcare generative AI firm Abridge recently cut its workforce as part of an "organization-wide realignment," the company confirmed to Fierce Healthcare on Friday.

The company did not disclose how many staff were impacted by the layoffs. Abridge, founded in 2018, has raised more than $750 million in venture capital funding to date. The company works with more than 300 health systems and is projected to support more than 100 million clinical conversations this year.

"We’re in a rare moment in health care and AI, and we’re realigning from a position of strength to flatten our organization and build and deliver products faster. This realignment will enable us to continue to grow, hire in priority areas, and invest in upcoming opportunities," the company noted in a statement provided to Fierce Healthcare.

Abridge remarked it was supporting staff impacted by the cuts with "meaningful transition packages and outplacement transition support.".

In a recent development, "Abridge is growing rapidly, reflected in both revenue growth and customer demand, and our pace of product development has accelerated significantly. As an AI-native firm, we are realigning teams across the organization to further increase our pace of innovation. Abridge remains very well capitalized, and continues to hold more than a majority of the capital it has raised to date," the company mentioned.

Healthcare startup Heidi reduced its headcount by 18%, the company's CEO and co-founderTom Kelly revealed in a LinkedIn post on Thursday.

Sources indicate that the firm did not disclose how many employees were impacted or what roles were cut. Heidi has more than 600 employees, so the cuts impacted about 108 staff.

The manufacturer, which first rolled out in Australia, initially started as an ambient AI medical scribe and then expanded into point-of-care clinical guidelines with Heidi Evidence and AI hardware (Remote) for clinical work as well as a voice-to-text feature, called Dictate. Heidi says it now supports around 2.8 million patient interactions each week in 110 languages from 190 countries.

"In the last few weeks, we reflected carefully on how we're structured, and we weren't putting our investment into the right teams and markets to make the most of our continuing growth. It's painful, but it's what we need to do now to continue growing swiftly and deliver on our plans for next year," Kelly wrote in his LinkedIn post.

The company is providing severance and benefits packages that vary by country but "exceed statutory requirements in every location," he wrote.

"Heidi is growing rapidly because clinicians around the world need and want our technology. We are investing in expanding our products, markets and team, and now support three million patient interactions every week. Our team has helped make that possible," Kelly wrote in a note to staff posted to the company's website. "After reviewing our priorities in detail, we’ve made difficult choices about where to focus our team and investment to deliver the greatest impact for customers going forward. That means bringing more customer support into product, bringing R&D together in one roadmap and giving our latest product businesses clearer ownership and dedicated teams.".

According to recent reports, also this week, Kelly announced that two of Heidi’s three co-founders, Waleed Mussa and Lu Yui. are preparing to leave the startup. "Waleed and Yu built Heidi with me, and it’s going to be really hard for all of us to continue without them. They’re leaving for different reasons, with their transitions happening over the coming weeks and months," Kelly wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Mussa is leaving to spend more time with his family, while Yui will transition into an advisory role focused on models and hardware through the end of March next year, Kelly wrote.

In September, Heidi landed $340 million to fuel its push beyond clinical documentation into AI-powered workflow automation and agentic capabilities for clinicians. The company raised $100 million series C funding. Alongside the equity round, Heidi also secured a $240 million growth investment led by General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund.

Children's Mercy, a pediatric health system based in Kansas City, Missouri, confirmed to press that it is cutting 115 positions, or about 1.2% of its total workforce.

The organization, in a statement, attributed the decision to "rising costs and reimbursement that has not kept pace." Among those affected, "most are non-clinical administrative, leadership and support roles," the statement reads.

Concurrent with the cuts was word that 473 of the system's revenue cycle and scheduling employees are shifting over to revenue cycle management vendor Ensemble, where they'll continue to work with Children's Mercy.

In April, the children's hospital unveiled plans to build a new acute patient tower at its flagship location in response to "increasing demand for highly specialized pediatric care as general hospitals nationwide reduce pediatric capacity." The project will expand total capacity by 25% to 30%, cost more than $1 billion and target a 2031 completion.

Rural Colorado nonprofit Montrose Regional Health, which includes a single 75-bed hospital and other clinical locations, declared this week a restructuring that eliminated 77 positions.

Of these, 43 were vacant and 34 were filled by current employees. Nearly half of the total positions were direct patient care roles, and 12 were leadership.

The system, in a release, noted its volumes have grown about 10% over the past year while commercial reimbursement stayed flat and expenses rose. Its decision came after restricting hiring and capital spending, cost reduction efforts and other measures to reduce losses and limit outstanding insurance payments for care already delivered, and will save over $8 million annually.

Recent findings suggest that the system said it does not have other workforce reductions planned at this time. The changes are not expected to affect "critical hospital-based services," though some service lines will be changing as part of the restructuring.

Recent findings suggest that specialty cancer care provider City of Hope filed a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification outlining intends to permanently lay off 73 employees, effective Nov. 24.

The organization, in a statement to Becker's, stated most of those affected work in business support and will receive support services like transition benefits and severance. The cuts will not directly affect patient care, they said.

Kaiser Permanente is laying off 147 workers across multiple Northern and Southern California locations, the country's largest nonprofit health system reported in Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification filings.

The reductions are effective on Nov. 20, and per the filing affect workers reporting to corporate and administrative offices.

The system, in statements to press, affirmed that the affected positions "do not provide direct patient care." The organization said some workers are looking at other openings within the system, though severance, career support and outplacement services are also being extended to others "where appropriate.".

SAC Health, a San Bernadino nonprofit chain of clinics, laid off 52 more workers shortly after a prior round of 49 cuts.

It has been revealed that the changes were reported in a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification filing and, in a prior internal memo and more recent statement to press, described the decision as necessary to strengthen operations. Both rounds of cuts involved nonclinical workers, with the former closely following the closure of two clinics.

The organization stated that patient care and services are continuing through the latest cuts without interruption, and, in an internal memo provided to employees, that no additional reorganization is planned.

In a recent development, catholic Health is eliminating 40 positions across five of its locations and realigning 34 other roles, according to a Sept. 22 press release shared with Fierce Healthcare.

The layoffs affect both union and non-union positions at Catholic Health’s Administrative and Regional Training Center, Mercy Hospital of Buffalo, Mount St. Mary’s Hospital, Sisters of Charity Hospital and St. Joseph Campus.

The health system is working with affected employees to review potential placement opportunities in current openings, the announcement said.

Recent findings suggest that moreover, 34 positions within Mercy Hospital are being realigned as “volumes surge” in its emergency department. Impacted employees will be able to transition directly into current vacancies within the hospital.

According to recent reports, “These are difficult decisions because they affect valued members of our Catholic Health family who have contributed greatly to our organization and the communities we serve,” noted Joyce Markiewicz, Catholic Health president and CEO, in a statement. “We are committed to treating every affected associate with dignity, compassion, and respect while ensuring Catholic Health remains strong and positioned to fulfill our mission well into the future.”.

Sources indicate that peaceHealth is planning to cut 150 positions across its facilities on Nov. 20, according to a notice filed with the Washington State Employment Security Department.

Bumping rights do not exist for any impacted positions, the Sept. 17 notice noted.

Fierce Healthcare has reached out to PeaceHealth for additional comment.

Elevance Health is laying off 216 positions in Louisiana as it prepares for its contract expiration with Medicaid in the state.

The organization disclosed the aims in a Sept. 15 notice (PDF), in which it stated the cuts would be effective Dec. 31. Louisiana’s Medicaid contract with Healthy Blue is set to expire the same day.

“We are focused on supporting our associates through this transition with clear communication, career resources and redeployment opportunities across Elevance Health wherever possible,” the tech giant remarked in a statement to Fierce Healthcare. “We are grateful for their dedication to Louisiana Medicaid members since 2017.”.

Latest Hampshire's Dartmouth Health noted it notified 124 workers that their positions had been eliminated, while also shuttering 303 open roles at the Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center and Dartmouth Hitchcock Clinics Southern Region.

In a recent development, the adjustments, it stated, will see executive and administrative leadership roles consolidated and "select programs" eliminated or affected, including Tele-ICU and Tele-ED, the New England Alliance for Health and some in-house employee training programs. The system said it does not expect the changes to harm patients.

“The employees affected by these changes have made meaningful contributions to Dartmouth Health, our patients and our communities,” Joanne M. Conroy, M.D., CEO and president of Dartmouth Health, stated in a statement. “Some have spent many years serving this organization. The decision to eliminate a position or program does not diminish the value of the work these colleagues have done and the contributions they have made.”.

Those affected by the cuts will be "offered resources, transition support and opportunities to pursue other roles within the health system," the system said.

According to recent reports, dartmouth Health noted that its operating expenses, particularly around labor, supply and drug costs, have outpaced patient revenues. Ahead of the cuts, it mentioned it has already worked to reduce some expenses by reducing travel and conference participation, reducing staffing reliance on traveler positions and strategic capital deployment to expand capacity and meet demand.

Recent findings suggest that A restructuring at University of Vermont Health will see 199 positions eliminated in late October, about 55 of which will be reconfigured into new positions, leadership announced in a Sept. 15 staff email and confirmed to press.

Sources indicate that the changes are a second round of layoffs for the academic system, when another restructuring saw 142 roles condensed into 66. Leadership attributed both to state mandates to reduce spending and other financial pressures.

Some displaced medical staff will be able to apply for other roles at the system, Leffler stated, and include leadership along with others. More than half of the affected roles are at the system's main medical center.

Sources indicate that "As we’ve discussed in our town hall meetings, our health system is facing a major budget shortfall, and we’re relying on our savings to pay the bills," system CEO and University of Vermont Medical Center President Stephen Leffler, M.D., wrote to staff. "That can’t continue.".

Recent findings suggest that some displaced medical staff will be able to apply for other roles at the system, Leffler noted, and include leadership along with others. More than half of the affected roles are at the system's main medical center.

Leffler also noted that the organization has cut 17% of its executive positions in the past year, axed "at-risk pay" for leaders and will be withholding raises for "most" senior leaders.

Conifer Health Solutions, the revenue cycle business of for-profit Tenet Healthcare, intends to permanently lay off 1,037 employees as a result of its breakup with CommonSpirit Health, according to a mandatory notice filing with the Texas Workforce Commission.

Sources indicate that the layoffs are set to begin on Nov. 2, according to the WARN filing, and involve workers who report to Tenet’s corporate headquarters in Dallas. Affected workers are not represented by a union and do not have any bumping rights. Read the full story here.

Hundreds of workers at nonprofit health system Trinity Health's Livonia, Michigan headquarters will be permanently laid off, according to a WARN filing with the state.

Recent findings suggest that trinity had signaled the staffing change back in June when it confirmed some in-house technology and information services work would be transitioned to an unspecified technology partner organization. That prior statement and the WARN filing outline positions that do not directly face patients.

Recent findings suggest that "The pace and complexity of health care technology are accelerating," Trinity mentioned in June. "Sustaining that pace is increasingly difficult for any single organization on its own. A partner whose core business is technology support gives us access to specialized expertise and innovation at the speed and scale health care now requires while strengthening service reliability.​".

Sources indicate that the cuts are scheduled to begin Oct. 25 and run through Nov. 29. Trinity previously suggested that some of the affected workers would have "opportunities for upcoming roles within Trinity Health and the partner organization along with transition support and resources.​".

For-profit hospital chain HCA Healthcare confirmed an unspecified number of layoffs in an emailed statement.

The system said the cuts represented "a small percentage of positions across our corporate office and support functions." It said the changes are a response to pressures like rising costs, shifting policy and increasing numbers of uninsured patients (HCA recently lowered its 2026 earnings forecast on worse-than-anticipated quarterly results).

The manufacturer noted it would be providing "a range of resources including severance and recruitment and outplacement support" to those affected, and noted that it is still hiring for other roles across its national footprint.

Academic health system Stanford Health Care has disclosed looks to trim 95 employees, or around 0.5% of its more than 18,000-person workforce.

Sources indicate that the organization disclosed the looks in an Aug. 28 California WARN filing, in which it remarked the cuts would be effective Nov. 2.

In a statement given to Fierce Healthcare, Stanford described the cuts as part of a regular review of its operations and patient needs.

None of the affected positions provide direct patient care, it said, and are located in its Technology and Digital Solutions department (79 workers, according to the WARN filing) as well as other administrative areas (16 workers).

"We are providing active support for redeployment within the organization where possible and opening new roles with the opportunity for impacted employees to apply," the statement reads.

Walnut Creek, California-based John Muir Health reported plans to lay off 78 workers, according to an Aug. 27 WARN filing .

The cuts will be effective Oct. 28 and span multiple sections of the nonprofit system. According to the filing, affected roles work in finance, human resources, marketing, IT, management and clinical care.

John Muir Health, in a statement, said that the layoffs impact about 1% of its workforce and "are mainly focused on leadership positions, employees in administrative services and employees who do not provide direct patient care.".

The system noted national and state policy headwinds like the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and California's 2030 seismic mandate, respectively, for its decision to proactively tighten its headcount.

Impacted employees have been notified, and any who do not find another position within the organization will receive a severance package offer, the statement reads.

Minnesota insurer UCare will layoff 102 employees as it continues to wind down its business.

In a recent development, per a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) posting on Aug. 3, the manufacturer will no longer support some of its Medicaid plans, which were sold to Medica, as of Oct. 1. As such, the layoffs are permanent.

Impacted employees include individuals working at its headquarters as well as workers who are primarily or exclusively remote.

Industry observers note that effected employees will work their last day in October, with one staying on until November, according to the notice. They will continue to be paid through the notice window.

UCare unveiled last November that it would begin to sunset its business operations following massive losses.

MaineHealth mentioned in a statement that it will be adjusting partis of its IT and analytics departments, leading to layoffs for 83 non-patient-facing employees.

Fifty-six of the cuts are among IT, while the remaining 27 in analytics stem from the consolidation of three separate teams into a single, 36-person unit. MaineHealth remarked that current employees in both departments "will participate in a selection process for roles in the redesigned organizations," but that "unfortunately not every affected care team member will have a role in the future-state IT and Analytics departments.".

The system employs about 24,000 people, and mentioned it will be "actively seeking opportunities elsewhere within" the organization "whenever possible before any employment separation occurs.".

MaineHealth mentioned the reorganization was prompted by changes in policy and reimbursement, as well as technology and patient demand.

In a recent development, tower Health filed a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification report with the state of Pennsylvania disclosing plans to lay off 160 at its Pottstown Hospital, effective Sept. 28.

The system, in a statement, said that the "difficult workforce decisions" come amid a multi-million-dollar overhaul that will expand the hospital's ED, boost behavioral health services and "enhancement portions of the hospital while realigning certain services to better reflect current patient demand and the realities of today's healthcare environment.".

Recent findings suggest that the statement did not outline any potential separation benefits being provided to those affected. The cuts represent over a fifth of the hospital's total headcount.

Wellstar Health System laid off 761 workers yesterday “following a comprehensive review of our organization,” the Georgia nonprofit confirmed to Fierce Healthcare.

Sources indicate that the cuts translate to roughly 2% of the organization’s 35,000-plus workforce and excluded any frontline care roles, Wellstar said. Rather, the layoffs “impact our corporate and shared services functions, as well as certain administrative roles within Wellstar Medical Group,” it said in the statement. Read more.

Novant Health confirmed to press it would be eliminating 31 jobs across the organization as part of an effort "to modernize our revenue cycle operations.".

The cuts are intended to head off redundancy at the 44,000-person system, and part of a regular evaluation of organizational structure, it told press.

"Decisions affecting team members are never made lightly," a spokesperson said. "While these changes are necessary to help ensure the long-term sustainability of our organization and our ability to serve patients, we recognize the impact on those affected and are committed to providing transition support. We are grateful for their contributions to Novant Health and our patients.".

Two Dignity Health hospitals, part of CommonSpirit Health, reported layoffs affecting 139 workers in recent WARN filings.

Fifty-seven of those cuts are at Bakersfield Memorial Hospital, in central California, with the remaining 82 at Los Angeles' California Hospital Medical Center.

It has been revealed that A representative for CommonSpirit confirmed the layoffs and in a statement said the organization was "realigning our resources and enhancing operational efficiencies" for the long term. The statement did not address any potential separation benefits or services.

According to recent reports, "At Bakersfield Memorial Hospital and California Hospital Medical Center, we are committed to delivering exceptional care and being a strong, sustainable partner in the health of our communities," the statement read. "Maintaining this commitment is difficult given the financial landscape impacting healthcare systems across the country which have impacted our business as well.".

Roseville, California-based Adventist Health confirmed 132 layoffs stemming from the system's decision to centralize quality, risk management, infection prevention and accreditation functions that were previously handled at the hospital level.

The cuts span several hospitals, according to a WARN filing. Of those affected, 109 have been offered new roles at the system.

Industry observers note that "To ensure we have strong accountability and deep expertise in these key functions, we have worked thoughtfully to create alignment of positions and centralization of roles. This fresh structure will advance our mission of compassionate, whole-person care—connecting dedicated local team members with best practices from system-level experts.".

Central Oregon's St. Charles Health System has overhauled its leadership structure, announcing the elimination of 22 filled and 23 open supervisor and above roles "in support services areas of the organization.".

It has been revealed that the cuts do not impact any direct patient care positions, and are hitting less than 1% of the four-hospital nonprofit's total workforce. It said the decision was made in response to the rapid growth in scale and demand its seen in recent years, and a need to adjust its structure for continuing increases.

Industry observers note that “The changes we are making today are about setting ourselves up for a more sustainable and scalable structure for the future and I want to reassure our community that St. Charles is strong, stable and committed to meeting community needs,” Michael Hartke, incoming president and CEO, stated in the announcement.

University of Missouri Health Care (MU Health Care) shared news of an "organizational redesign" that includes a 74-employee workforce reduction.

The cuts largely landed in non-clinical and administrative areas, with the system noting that "in some areas, staffing levels exceeded those of comparable organizations, while in others, operational assessments identified opportunities to add positions and better align resources with patient and operational needs.".

Those affected were offered transition resources, such as benefits continuation and other internal job opportunities, with the notice highlighting more than 500 other positions that are presently open across the system.

"Healthcare is changing rapidly, and our organization must evolve with it," Ric Ransom, CEO, said in the announcement. "These decisions are difficult, but they are necessary to ensure MU Health Care remains strong, competitive and capable of serving patients and communities for generations to come.".

Sources indicate that other changes at the system include tweaks to various employee benefit programs that would require board approval "including retirement contributions," and the closure of four retail health clinics. At the same time, it noted a strategy to boost other benefits like dependent care assistance and expansions of some urgent care and imaging services.

Industry observers note that "These actions are not simply about reducing costs," mentioned Ransom. "They are about aligning our organization with the realities of modern health care, improving how we serve patients and ensuring we can continue investing in our people, our mission and the communities that rely on us.".

Lovelace Health System has laid off "approximately 43 positions," or about 1.6% of its local workforce, a representative told Fierce Healthcare in a statement.

Sources indicate that the cuts are primarily in administrative and support positions, and the system looked to curb the impact by placing some of its employees in other open roles, the representative stated. The system is "supporting affected team members through this transition," but did not specify whether that includes severance or other benefits.

"These are difficult decisions, and we don't take them lightly," the statement reads. "Like health systems across the country, we are facing rising costs, shifting payor dynamics and a challenging policy environment. These actions reflect deliberate steps to manage costs and ensure our structure keeps pace with current realities.".

Lovelace is a five-hospital system based in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and is owned and operated by publicly traded for-profit Ardent Healthcare.

BSA Health System, a three-hospital system serving Texas' Panhandle region, is cutting 29 of its staff, or 1% of its local workforce, according to a local media report.

The system is part of Ardent Healthcare, and appears to be providing press with a near-identical statement on the decision as Lovelace Health System (above) pointing to "rising costs, shifting payor dynamics and a challenging policy environment." Fierce Healthcare has reached out to BSA Health System for confirmation.

UPMC, the nonprofit system that stands as Pennsylvania's largest non-governmental employer, confirmed it is cutting about 200 employees and shuttering 300 open positions that were not in active recruitment.

A spokesperson organization, which employs about 100,000 total and operates more than 40 hospitals, stated the reductions are "primarily among those who are not in clinical or member-facing roles." The system will also be giving "enhanced severance pay and benefits coverage for affected employees," they said.

In a recent development, UPMC recorded $33.6 billion in total operating revenue across 2025 as well as a 0.9% operating margin. The layoffs come about two years after the organization conducting a more sweeping reduction of 1,100 workers two years ago, noted one of the nurse unions active in UPMC's hospitals.

Recent findings suggest that "In that previous round of cuts, we lost many experienced and valued clinicians with roles in direct patient care and nurse education," Michelle Hart, a neonatal nurse practitioner and member of Magee Nurses and Advanced Practitioners United, SEIU Healthcare PA, said in a statement. "When UPMC reduces staff, those duties often then fall on nurses when we already do not have enough time with our patients to provide the level of care we believe in. ... UPMC cannot continue to prioritize branding, construction and executive compensation over investing in frontline staff.".

University of Vermont Health remarked this week it has eliminated 142 positions in Vermont and Northern New York, of which 76 are permanent deletions and 66 will be reposted with adjusted job descriptions.

The academic system said most of the changes weren't in areas providing direct patient care, but that some comprised "targeted clinical changes where necessary." It added that more employees were informed that their positions or departments are in the midst of reorganization.

The organization attributed its decisions to "significant financial shortfalls.".

Sources indicate that “These are extremely difficult decisions because of their impact on our valued colleagues,” UVM Health CEO Stephen Leffler, M.D., said in a release on the cuts. “We must make these hard choices to ensure we can continue to provide high-quality care that is accessible and more affordable for the communities we serve.”.

It has been revealed that UVM Health said it's working with employees' unions through the layoffs, and that those affected are being offered transition support and a chance to apply to other roles. Its cuts follow smaller cuts at its Northern New York earlier this year that affected nine workers, and a more substantial round last July that hit 146 positions.

Centra Health, a nonprofit system serving central and southern Virginia, shared news of a restructuring that will lead to "approximately 90" layoffs, or about 1% of its total workforce.

Of those affected, the system remarked 35 are being offered other open positions for which they are qualified. Eligible employees will receive severance as well as continued healthcare coverage under COBRA. Centra added that it has "used natural attrition" over the past several months, deciding not to refill positions as former employees left.

Centra noted the restructure is part of a broader initiative focused on spotting redundancies and efficiencies, "particularly in administrative functions," and will help "adapt to the significant pressures facing healthcare providers including reductions in government reimbursements, economic challenges, shifting demographics and evolving technologies.".

Baptist Health has shared word that it is eliminating around 70 workers in Arkansas' Fort Smith area.

A statement on the decision shared with press pointed to "a sustained decrease in service volumes and the duplication of certain roles." The system added that the cuts will not affect care services, and that those impacted will receive severance and job placement services.

Of note, the news comes less than two months after Baptist announced plans to ax 150 other employees in the same area as a result of service line changes.

Optum will layoff 58 workers across three divisions based in the Garden State, according to Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act notices.

The largest share of those layoffs are at Optum Services, where 36 positions will be eliminated. Five jobs will be cut at Optum Care, and 17 people will be laid off at Optum Select Management. The layoffs are effective on Aug. 26, according to the document.

Optum had not yet returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Washington Regional Medical System, northwest Arkansas' largest healthcare provider, revealed a "strategic organizational restructuring" it noted will reduce its workforce by 86 people.

The nonprofit remarked it will be consolidating certain management and support functions, while also redesigning its workflows to reduce administrative burdens. The decision is a response to financial pressures including heightened labor and supply costs as well as "continued reimbursement challenges.".

According to recent reports, “We are all evaluating our business and implementing significant operational changes,” Washington Regional President and CEO Lucas Campbell, M.D., in the announcement. “By restructuring our management operations and consolidating roles, Washington Regional will reduce redundancies and optimize efficiency while still providing the high-quality care our community has come to expect.”.

The system remarked there will be no disruptions in patient care due to the changes. It did not specify whether benefits, severance or other support is being provided to affected employees.

Care New England said it has laid off more than 30 nonclinical and leadership jobs "as part of a restructuring in response to ongoing financial pressures that continue to strain hospitals and healthcare providers throughout Rhode Island.".

Employees affected by the restructuring will received unspecified "resources and assistance" from the system, according to the announcement.

Care New England said it has been working to address an estimated $20 million budget shortfall for the 2026 fiscal year. Its announcement of the cuts pointed to low Medicaid reimbursement rates, rising expenses and greater demand for uncompensated care, and included calls for state leaders to back a proposed funding package.

It has been revealed that “Without meaningful action, Rhode Island risks continued erosion of healthcare access, longer emergency room wait times, reduced services, and additional job losses throughout the healthcare sector," President and CEO Michael Wagner, M.D., stated. "We urge state leaders to prioritize investments that strengthen healthcare and protect access to care for all Rhode Islanders.”.

Closures and consolidations across 10 Intermountain Health clinics in Montana and Colorado will hit 93 of the nonprofit system's employees, according to statements given to press.

Industry observers note that in Montana, the system intends to close a family medicine clinic and "shift the model of care" at four of its other clinics. In Colorado, Intermountain plans to close two occupational health clinics and a sports medicine clinic, while also planning to fold an endocrinology clinic into a primary care clinic and shuttering some services at an obesity management clinic.

In a recent development, forty-one of the cuts are among "leader and staff member roles" in Montana, with Colorado employees comprising the remainder. The changes are scheduled to take effect from early June through late July, depending on the site.

Intermountain's statement chalked the decisions up to strengthening "long-term financial sustainability in an increasingly volatile healthcare industry." It noted employees whose roles are impacted may apply for other open positions, and that they will be given access to "transition support, career assistance, severance (where applicable) and benefits guidance.".

Sources indicate that health tech company Innovaccer reduced its workforce, primarily impacting positions outside the United States, the company confirmed to Fierce Healthcare. Inc42 reported that the company laid off 340 employees, impacting staff in India and the U.S.

In a statement, Innovaccer said the workforce reduction was related to its shift to AI-enabled operations.

Industry observers note that "As an AI-native health technology manufacturer, Innovaccer is applying its own automation principles internally. We are building an organization that is lean, fast and focused, which prioritizes speed and measurable outcomes for our customers," the company said.

It's the company's third layoff round in the past four years, Inc42 reported.

In a recent development, the tech giant, founded in 2014, built software solutions that aggregate patient data across care settings and systems. Innovaccer secured a $275 million series F funding round in January 2025 to invest in artificial intelligence with the goal of becoming a “one-stop shop” for healthcare AI solutions.

The tech giant has raised $675 million to date with a post-money valuation of approximately $3.45 billion following its series F round.

According to recent reports, in September, it acquired Story Health, a digital specialty care platform with health system inroads. That deal was preceded by a number of other acquisitions, including Humbi AI, an actuarial software, services and analytics tech giant, in January 2025 and two companies in 2024: Cured, a digital marketing and CRM platform for healthcare, and Pharmacy Quality Solutions, a pharmacy-payer performance technology.

Forty jobs are in the firing line of a rehashed behavioral health model at Providence Sacred Heart Medical Center.

It has been revealed that the Spokane, Washington facility will transition emergency department psych triage services into a fresh department staffed by licensed therapists beginning July 14, Providence mentioned in a release given to press. Other mental health support roles in the ED and adult geriatric psych unit will also change over to a new staffing model that relies on certified nursing assistants with specialized behavioral health training, it said.

There will be no interruption in behavioral service availability during the shift, Providence stated.

The nation's largest for-profit health system confirmed Monday an undisclosed number of non-clinical layoffs.

The cuts, according to a statement, "represent a small portion of our workforce," which exceeded 300,000 people as of earlier this year. On the other hand, Nashville Business Journal, which first reported the layoffs, cited two unnamed sources who described the cuts as "significant in scale.".

It has been revealed that HCA remarked in its statement it is supporting affected colleagues and, where possible, helping connect them with other opportunities within and outside of HCA Healthcare. We continue to recruit and hire for a wide range of clinical and non-clinical roles across the U.S. to support the care we deliver to patients and the communities we serve.".

Service line changes at Baptist Health will hit 150 employees' roles over the next 60 days.

Industry observers note that the cuts are tied to the system's Baptist Health Fort Smith hospital, which the company noted has lost a cumulative $127 million from 2018 through March 2026. To avoid closure, services including obstetrics, oncology, nephrology, pulmonary and infectious disease care have or will soon wind down, with other affiliated clinics also set to shutter.

The 150 affected employees, among which are 10 physicians, are being offered 60 days of severance, career transition support and opportunities to join other roles at the system, Baptist Health noted.

"By stabilizing our foundation now, we stop the cycle of unsustainable losses and create a platform from which we can eventually grow and even add services back," the organization wrote in a statement for press.

Oregon Health & Science University said it is cutting 59 positions tied to its Knight Cancer Institute.

Most of the layoffs, 30, affect the Cancer Early Detection Advanced Research Center. The organization attributed the decisions to "a rough climate for research funding.".

Nine employees at two University of Vermont Health hospitals in northern New York were reportedly eliminated in response to cost and policy pressures.

Two of the affected workers were at Alice Hyde Medical Center and seven worked at Champlain Valley Physicians Hospital.

UnityPoint Health, which employs 31,000 people, remarked this week it will be eliminating 207 of its IT roles amid a transition of their responsibilities to third-party vendors.

The outsourcing is focused on IT and revenue cycle functions and driven by financial pressures "like many health systems across the country," President and CEO Scott Kizer said in a statement given to press. Additional cuts are on the way for the system's revenue cycle workers, though how many will be affected has not yet been determined.

Those being laid off are being provided with severance, benefits continuation and other career transition support.

Baylor Scott & White Health Plan, the insurance arm of the nonprofit Texas system, shared plans exit the individual marketplaces as well as Medicaid, a move it mentioned will impact 321 jobs.

Baylor Scott & White Health noted it will focus on supporting the affected individuals through the transition, including career guidance, priority opportunities elsewhere within the system, and funded upskilling for in-demand clinical roles. It also noted that it continues to hire for patient care roles elsewhere in the system.

Advanced Specialty Hospitals of Toledo's May 1 closure will see 116 workers permanently laid off, effective June 8, according to a Workers Adjustment and Retraining Notification filing.

The affected workers, according to the notice, include 45 registered nurses as well as nurse aides, pharmacy technicians, speech language pathologists and other clinical and non-clinical job roles.

Greenwood Leflore Hospital, a publicly owned hospital with 25 licensed acute care beds and 24/7 emergency department, mentioned this week it would be laying off 86 employees, of whom 40 are part-time.

The decision is accompanied by immediate and planned service line closures including an after-hours clinic, wellness center, outpatient rehab and cardiac rehab, according to a statement given to press and other online notices. The hospital is left with about 425 employees plus 58 contracted workers.

The hospital, which serves an area of Mississippi with limited healthcare access, has been teetering financially for the past few years and had recently began exploring a deal to join the University of Mississippi Medical Center. This week's statement noted that the restructuring decisions were made "as the hospital prepares for either a transition of operations to a larger health system or a potential closure.".

UCI Health announced a strategic restructuring that will lay off about 1% of its workforce, or roughly 150 people.

In a recent development, the six-hospital academic system mentioned its effort will be combining position and better matching roles to its developing needs. Those affected "will receive comprehensive financial support, job placement services, and priority consideration for open positions across UCI Health as part of the organization’s realignment.".

The California organization cited federal funding shifts and insurance reimbursement changes for its restructuring, as well as patients' different approaches to care access.

“We approach this moment with respect and care, feeling deeply grateful for our co-workers’ vital contributions to our community and those we serve," Chad Lefteris, president and CEO of UCI Health, said. "We recognize that change impacts all of our co-workers. But this realignment is vital to ensuring our ability to continue meeting the evolving needs of the communities we serve.".

Bankrupt Fresh York system North Star Health Alliance noted in a release that it will be taking "additional operational restructuring actions" despite already conducting a prior round of layoffs near the top of the year affecting more than 100 people.

The system stated the "workforce adjustments" will span the organization, and target greater operational efficiency while preserving essential care access. It did not disclose how many employees will be affected.

In a recent development, “This is a difficult but necessary step as we move through the Chapter 11 process and continue strengthening our organization for the future,” remarked CEO Andrew Manzer. “Our focus remains on strengthening the organization so we can continue delivering high-quality care close to home.”.

Pharmacy giant Walgreens will eliminate jobs in two states as it adapts to cost pressures as a private tech giant under fresh owner Sycamore Partners.

A spokesperson for Walgreens confirmed the layoffs in a statement to Fierce Healthcare. Bloomberg reported that notices submitted in Illinois, where the company is headquartered, include 469 job cuts. A further 159 positions will be eliminated in Texas, according to the report.

"We’re focused on becoming America’s best retail pharmacy, beginning with improving the in‑store experience for our customers and patients," the spokesperson said. "To do this, we’ve made the difficult decision to simplify our organization in both the support center and with our field leadership to speed decision making and improve the service that millions of customers rely on every day.".

They added that the company will support employees in the transition.

Walgreens was purchased by Sycamore Partners last year after facing declining profitability.

Baystate Health, a five-hospital nonprofit system in Massachusetts, confirmed the reduction of 117 corporate positions, which it said is less than 1% of its total workforce.

The system, in a statement given to press, outlined "ever-increasing headwinds" ranging from rising supply expenses to expired Affordable Care Act subsidies to increased demand from patients covered by government plans.

Baystate did not outline specific affected roles, but mentioned those affected by the job cuts have been "notified with compassion and provided with support resources." The statement also described a decision to outsource clinical engineering to medical equipment management organization TRIMEDX, with Baystate's relevant team set to become employees of TRIMEDX beginning in May.

Nine-hospital nonprofit PeaceHealth filed a notice Wednesday that it plans to permanently eliminate 94 positions across its Washington facilities.

The layoffs are expected to to be effective by April 12, according to the notice, and a list of affected roles include clinical and non-clinical job titles. Some of the employees have union representation.

In a statement to press, a representative noted the cuts affect less than 1% of the system's workforce and reflectthe changing needs of our growing communities, ongoing financial pressures to reduce costs and our commitment to advancing the health and well-being of those we serve.”.

The reductions come just a few months after the system cut about 400 workers (2.5% of the workforce) and closed some open positions amid organizational adjustments. Prior to that it had cut 1% and instituted a partial hiring freeze in May.

Cigna is planning to eliminate about 2,000 jobs across its global footprint, accounting for about 3% of its total workforce.

Chatter across platforms like LinkedIn and Reddit have discussed the layoffs for several days. Benefits PRO reports that voluntary retirements were also offered to eligible employees.

It's unclear how many individuals are effected by the layoffs, and if any of the jobs were not filled.

According to recent reports, “As we drive greater efficiency across our business, we have made the difficult decision to reduce roles in our workforce," a Cigna spokesperson told Fierce Healthcare. "This decision was made with deliberate care and focus, and we are providing a package that includes a variety of transition services for impacted colleagues.”.

Unite Us, the tech company facilitating referrals to social services, laid off workers on Wednesday. The move affected about 20% of staff, or over 80 people, two people affected told Fierce Healthcare. The cuts primarily hit the product and customer support teams, they remarked.

The company did not confirm the number of people affected, but a spokesperson told Fierce Healthcare the move was a "targeted reduction." Unite Us is providing "career transition assistance" to those affected.

According to recent reports, "We can confirm that Unite Us remains in a strong, stable financial position. The recent changes allow us to better align our teams and investments with our core offerings and deliver outcomes for our state and healthcare partners," the spokesperson remarked in an email.

Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield will eliminate 242 positions, according to a WARN notice submitted this month in the Garden State.

A spokesperson for the insurer told Fierce Healthcare that the non-profit payer is staring down the same financial challenges that are impacting the industry writ large, and that it notified employees in November that it would conduct a restructuring in early 2026 that would lead to the elimination of about 300 positions.

The individuals impacted by the layoffs were notified on Monday, the spokesperson said. The insurer has trimmed its workforce by 8% accounting for this round of layoffs and other actions taken in 2025, they said.

In a recent development, "We do not take workforce reductions lightly," per the spokesperson. "Employees whose positions were eliminated were treated with fairness and respect and will receive a generous separation package.".

New York's Erie County Medical Center remarked it is laying off about 150 employees, or about 3% of its team.

The cuts are primarily in non-clinical roles, though a local nurses' union noted that some frontline clinicians were also affected. The hospital is also requiring one week of unpaid furlough in 2026 for its "management confidential employees.".

Sources indicate that the center's statement placed the blame on "inadequate reimbursements from both public and private payers," adding that "insurance companies continue to deny and delay payment for patient care services at an alarming rate. It stressed that it has not fully closed any of its programs, "but has made targeted reductions in services to meet patient demands and our financial realities.".

ECU Health, in eastern North Carolina, will be laying off 31 positions within its Access East program, which helps deliver non-medical and other complex care-management services to Medicaid recipients.

According to recent reports, the cuts stem from a decision by the state legislature not to fund the Healthy Opportunities Pilot program that supported its efforts. The system, in statements to press and a regulatory notice, remarked the terminations are set to go into effect on March 31, but that the organization is looking at other internal openings for those affected where possible.

Hennepin Healthcare, which operates HCMC in Minneapolis and a network of primary care clinics in Hennepin County, intends to cut 100 positions and shutter some services as it faces a massive budget shortfall.

The health system is making targeted service line adjustments as part of a broader, long-term effort to stabilize its finances and protect core clinical services and care capacity, the organization said in an announcement posted to its website on Monday.

It has been revealed that hennepin Healthcare will be closing or integrating some stand-alone clinics and services. The health system will close chiropractic and acupuncture services and refer patients to external providers and it is shuttering its sleep clinic. The system remarked it will continue to do sleep screening tests through primary care.

Sources indicate that senior and extended care also will be impacted as older adult patients will now be seen in primary care and nursing home services will be transitioned to other systems, the health system said. Patients needing pain treatments also will be transitioned to other providers. Medical and surgical services for weight management will be reduced and integrated into the Clinic and Specialty Center instead of operating as a stand-alone clinic.

Hennepin Healthcare runs Hennepin County Medical Center (HCMC), a Level I adult and pediatric trauma center and safety net hospital.

Earlier this month, the upcoming co-leaders at Hennepin Healthcare sent a message to workers saying job cuts and service reductions would be needed soon because of a cash-flow crisis, the Minnesota Star Tribune reported.

During a press conference Monday, Dr. Kevin Croston, the co-interim administrator of Hennepin Healthcare, told reporters that the health system is at the moment facing a financial crisis due to budget challenges and health insurer UCare closing, among other factors, Minnesota Public Radio reported.

The health system is trying to close a $50 million budget hole by the end of March, several media outlets reported.

Hennepin Healthcare also is confronting a projected $100 million loss in uncompensated care and a $1.7 billion reduction in Medicaid revenue over the next 10 years, MPR reported.

In a recent development, pomona Valley Hospital Medical Center shared plans to cuts 265 roles—128 via planned retirements and vacant position closures and the remaining 137 through layoffs and a reduction in hours. The layoffs will take effect by March 8, according to a WARN filing.

In a recent development, the 427-bed nonprofit, which employs about 4,000 people, cited federal and California reimbursement cuts for its decision as well as a budget shortfall of $40 million. The plan for job reductions and other measures was put together following a “thorough evaluation of operational requirements, organizational structure and redundancies in positions,” a spokesperson told press.

It has been revealed that the layoffs will take effect by March 8, according to a WARN filing. Those affected will receive severance and other support.

In a recent development, pomona Valley noted the reductions affect management as well as clinical and nonclinical roles but that patient care would not be affected. A labor union representing some of the hospital’s nurses told membership it plans to enforce protections outlined in its collective bargaining agreement, including an option for laid-off nurses to apply for and be given other open positions for which they are qualified.

Blue Cross of Idaho remarked it will be laying off fewer than 90 workers, a move the group said will allow it “to remain a strong, Idaho-based company” and better serve its nearly 600,000 members.

The insurer did not give details on specific roles affected to a timeline for the cuts. It had already reduced its head count by 135 early last year when the state health department passed it over for a dual-eligible contract.

Industry observers note that L.A. Care Health Plan will lay off 225 employees, about 3% of its workforce, on or before March 13.

Recent findings suggest that the country’s largest publicly operated health strategy remarked in a statement the decision stemmed from federal and state funding cuts, and that its restructure will strengthen critical capabilities and introduce upcoming roles to help do so. It also said it will provide transition support and resources to affected workers.

Trinity Health said it will be laying off about a tenth of its revenue cycle management team, instead outsourcing the work to a vendor in a bid to reduce costs.

The 92-hospital nonprofit system did not disclose how many workers are affected but stated the reductions affect workers in 15 states. The organization also did not share whether those losing their positions would receive a compensation package.

Alameda Health System will lay off about 250 employees across multiple locations.

In a recent development, A regulatory filing outlining most of these lists March 9 as the terminations’ date of effect. The California organization said its cuts will span several areas, and it is also offering voluntary resignations and retirements with financial incentives.

The reductions stem from impending funding cuts.

North Star Health Alliance declared layoffs affecting around 120 of its workers.

The Newly introduced York system told press its cuts will span clinical, nonclinical and management employees and be split roughly equally across its two main campuses. Those affected did not receive severance payments outside of what was obligated under their employment contracts.

The cuts come in the wake of a payment dispute between North Star and Upcoming York’s Department of Health related to the restructuring of its hospital into a critical access hospital and a co-located inpatient acute psychiatric hospital.

Vibra Healthcare will be laying off 310 employees when it closes Specialty Hospital of Portland, the state’s only long-term acute care facility, due to financial challenges.

The decision was declared in December but will take effect on or before Feb. 1, per a WARN filing. Leadership, nonclinical workers and clinical positions such as nurses and therapists who worked at the 73-bed facility are affected.

The American People Deserve a Better Deal.

Recent findings suggest that washington, DC — Today, the Senate passed the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026” following little debate and an insufficient amendment process. BAAJA will now go to the House of Representatives for consideration.

In response, Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford released the following statement:.

“While a rogue president is waging a war on clean energy, the Senate rushed a deeply flawed bill that furthers the buildout of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and Tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands, and endangers wildlife. The House of Representatives has an equal voice in the legislative process. They must reject the Senate’s fast-tracked bill and demand debate and consideration to deliver for the people, not corporate polluters and Donald Trump. The American people made a clear call merely weeks ago: our elected leaders must address soaring costs and a corrupt system that prioritizes corporate polluter profits over our health, our wallets, and our future.

“The Sierra Club thanks the Senators, Tribes, and advocates across the country who raised their voices in the fight to fix this bill. Americans deserve a better deal.”.

Stellantis Is Pulling Out Of Every Racing Series It Competes In Except NASCAR

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (432 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that stellantis is about to throw in the towel on just about every single one of its motorsports endeavors other than NASCAR...
  • The moves come as the automaker cuts costs across the board at the behest of CEO Antonio Filosa, according to Reuters.
  • This isn't the first time something like this has happened for Peugeot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that stellantis is about to throw in the towel on just about every single one of its motorsports endeavors other than NASCAR... which it just re-entered after a 14-year hiatus. On November 23, it's expected that the automaker will convene two extraordinary works council meetings with the ultimate outcome being a withdrawal. That means Peugeot would leave endurance racing (which admittedly hasn't been going too well), Citroën and Opel would drop out of Formula E, and Lancia's reborn rally team would bite the dust.

The moves come as the automaker cuts costs across the board at the behest of CEO Antonio Filosa, according to Reuters. He's doing what he can to turn the company around after years of falling sales and weakening profitability. Earlier this year, Filosa launched a broad efficiency drive, known as the "Value Creation Program," and it targets about $6.6 billion in cost savings by 2028. Autocar reports that Stellantis Motorsport costs about $330 million a year to run, and cutting it could help with Stellantis' finances in Europe, where it just lost $341 million in the third quarter alone.

This isn't the first time something like this has happened for Peugeot. Its former owners, PSA, quit the 24 Hours of Le Mans back in 2012 in an effort to save cash, and it didn't rejoin until 2022.

Recent findings suggest that it is, nevertheless, still strange timing. As I mentioned, Dodge just re-entered NASCAR. On top of that, French outlet L'Automobile reports that Peugeot has a redesigned 9x8 for its 2027 WEC endurance program and Citroën and Opel have been working on their newly introduced Gen4 car for Formula E with new technical partners. It's likely that the team that runs Citroën, MSG Racing, will continue with a new sponsor.

Industry observers note that hell, Open is technically making its debut in FE this upcoming season. It was just announced in March of this year when the brand signed a four-year contract to compete with the latest Gen4 cars.

Lancia's WRC re-entry is another sacrificial lamb at the altar of financial prudence. The Lancia Corse HF team started in the WRC2 category this year, Autocar reports. It entered its gas-powered Ypsilon Rally2 HF Integrale, and it has even racked up a few wins. More likely than not, customer teams will continue to be supported, though.

Sources indicate that motorsports are usually what's first to get cut when an automaker is struggling. Earlier this year, Alpine dropped out of WEC, citing a tough market, and Porsche did the same thing back in 2025.

Sources indicate that deployment services are becoming the real battleground in AI infrastructure as buyers discover that shipping hardware is only half the job. With GPU supply tight and refresh cycles accelerating, neoclouds and enterprises are judging suppliers on how promptly an AI factory actually goes live.

“It’s not just enough to deliver to the customers. They want it online as quickly as possible. Time is money,” Thauberger stated.

Thauberger spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how deployment services are driving the race to time to online and how liquid cooling retrofits help older facilities take on modern AI racks. (* Disclosure below.).

Recent findings suggest that customers are leaning on suppliers for far more than boxes. Allocation and deployment services are the two biggest requests Supermicro hears, and its service teams bring systems up, run customer workloads and hand off only once everything is running, Thauberger explained.

According to recent reports, “We know that we’re in a constrained environment. There’s no secret on that. So customers are basically asking Supermicro how quickly you can get allocation, how quickly you can bring it online, and how quickly you can have people out on site to deploy those,” Thauberger remarked.

According to recent reports, older facilities pose another hurdle. Many weren’t designed for the liquid cooling and power density of modern AI racks, so Supermicro offers retrofit options such as sidecars and in-row coolant distribution units, according to Thauberger. The organization has also added pre-assembled AI racks to its building-block lineup to shorten installs.

“We have the largest liquid cooling capacity based in California. We’re a U.S.-headquartered company, and the ability for us to have as much liquid cooling capacity as we have inside the U.S. allows us to deploy to these AI factories quick inside the United States,” Thauberger stated.

#18942. Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027

Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1410 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fiercehealthcare

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Federal health officials are focused on rebuilding trust with the public and working across the aisle with the new Congress.
  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F.
  • In a fireside chat, a chipper Schwartz tried to answer a tough line of questioning about Americans’ loss of trust in her agency, controversial vaccine changes, measles and other public health challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Federal health officials are focused on rebuilding trust with the public and working across the aisle with the new Congress.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., spoke at the Milken Institute’s Future of Health Summit last week in Washington, D.C. Over 1,200 attendees gathered at the event, the theme of which was “better health within reach.”.

In a fireside chat, a chipper Schwartz tried to answer a tough line of questioning about Americans’ loss of trust in her agency, controversial vaccine changes, measles and other public health challenges.

When asked about her potential disagreements with Kennedy, Schwartz stated, “I disagree all the time. He’s a lawyer, I’m a lawyer. […] What I love about the secretary is that he listens to those disagreements. He's not someone who just states, ‘No, I don't have room for that.’ He really does value differing opinions.”.

In a recent development, the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, global health officials unveiled just this week. On that issue, Schwartz stressed the importance of supporting CDC’s state partners on awareness, prevention and surveillance efforts.

It has been revealed that “MMR is the number one way to prevent measles,” Schwartz noted. Today’s outbreaks “happen in communities that are very close-knit communities … that typically do not and have not vaccinated their children,” she said. Most cases are currently among kids over the age of five and adults, according to Schwartz.

Under Schwartz’s leadership, the CDC changed its method of reporting measles deaths from real-time reporting by state public health departments to death certificate data, which can face multi-month lags. Schwartz is being investigated by Energy & Commerce Committee Democrats who, during a briefing on CDC’s alleged suppression of the total number of national measles deaths on its dashboard, have called her unresponsive and misleading.

Sources indicate that “As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of measles deaths that CDC reports to the public, concealing the fact that 10 people have died of measles-related deaths this year alone,” the Committee leaders wrote (PDF) in a letter on Tuesday. “We are expanding our investigation to examine the threat your actions pose to Americans’ health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required.”.

During her fireside chat, Schwartz acknowledged that "we've lost trust not only externally with the American public, but also internally with the team that works at the CDC,” she said. To address this, Schwartz wants the public to understand that CDC follows the science, is being transparent and “leading with humility.” She pointed to COVID-era “arrogance” from institutions, directing at instead of conversing with the public.

“I want to be a CDC director that really has a conversation with the American public,” Schwartz said.

Internally, the first priority is to add stability to the body, including hiring leaders within the agency so they have a permanent leadership role. The CDC has also created a strategic hiring blueprint for 2027 with the input of staff and is looking to its “force extenders” like epidemic intelligence officers and its Public Health Associate Program.

On how she’s planning to work with the newly introduced majority-Democratic Congress, Schwartz noted she was encouraged to see more Congress members coming in with a healthcare background, “who understand how these policies will impact patients.” She remarked is eager to work with the Congressional Doctors Caucus and to work with both sides of the aisle.

“I know that we may not agree on every issue, but I do think there's a common ground where we can actually focus on really trying to make Americans healthy again,” she said.

One of her priorities for 2027 is having a “21st-century CDC” by bringing innovation into the public health sphere. She called out the Biothreat Radar, a proposed wastewater surveillance program about which she recently spoke with Sen. Andy Kim (D-Upcoming Jersey). The program’s proposed (PDF) budget is $52 million. The CDC has also tentatively put out a call for new Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) members, which will depend on a final ruling from the appellate court in the agency’s favor.

At the Summit, Schwartz’s comments did not necessarily satisfy some of the attendees. When asked by Fierce Healthcare for his impressions of the interview, a public health worker in the room who did not wish to be named called her a “traitor.".

In his fireside chat closing out the Summit, Secretary Kennedy primarily spoke about food and obesity.

One of HHS' most consequential accomplishments during his tenure, Kennedy remarked, has been changing the dietary guidelines to be “science-based.” Earlier this year, the White House released upcoming federal dietary guidelines, calling for prioritizing quality protein, healthy fats, fruits, vegetables and whole grains, while avoiding highly processed foods and refined carbs.

The agency is focused on transforming food across a number of sectors, including in Head Start programs—free federal early childhood programs—which have received about $151 million in supplemental HHS awards to strengthen nutrition services. HHS is also focused on rolling out healthy food options in the military, Kennedy said, and within SNAP by allowing states to request waivers to restrict what SNAP dollars are spent on. As of this summer, HHS has launched a Make Hospital Food Healthier Pledge, challenging hospitals to put nutrition at the center of patient care. HHS has also encouraged medical schools to increase their number of education hours on nutrition from an average of two to 40 hours, Kennedy said.

“Real” food sales in grocery stores, Kennedy claimed, went up 8% this year, while obesity rates have dropped by 7%. He acknowledged that the drop in obesity rates is more likely due to GLP-1 access rather than healthier eating. “If we can reduce obesity, we can reduce our healthcare costs,” he remarked, praising Trump’s Most Favored Nation negotiations for lowering the price of drugs like Ozempic.

Recent findings suggest that “We reward people at every level—the hospitals, the providers, other providers, doctors, insurance companies, pharmaceutical companies—we reward them financially for keeping people sick. And as long as those financial incentives are in place, we are going to be operating a sick-care system rather than a healthcare system,” Kennedy mentioned. HHS has started to change that by shifting more to value-based care, he added, so stakeholders get paid to keep patients healthy “rather than being paid to keep them sick.”.

Sources indicate that when asked what he wants his legacy as Health Secretary to be, Kennedy echoed Schwartz on the idea of following science. “What I want to do is to end corporate capture and the politicization of science … that Americans once again trust the regulatory agencies, they trust the science that’s coming from them,” he mentioned.

He referred to newer guidelines meant to encourage extra transparency from researchers. In 2026, the HHS Scientific Integrity Policy was updated (PDF) to support publishing raw data and code in publicly accessible repositories, preregistering study protocols and transparently reporting all results.

He remarked he wants "to make sure that we’re not kowtowing to the food industry, the pharmaceutical industry, all these people who are at the trough taking on the $2.3 trillion that my agency gives out every year. And that instead, that Americans believe that this agency is devoted to their health, that they trust it, and that we are doing the science that we need to find out what is making them sick so that we can all eliminate it as a society.”.

In a recent development, kennedy's interview at the event did not touch on measles or vaccine policy, where the secretary's policies and communications have garnered broader criticism and controversy than his views on nutrition. Tuesday's announcement that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination status garnered a fresh call for Kennedy's resignation among his critics, including the Democratic Doctors Caucus.

Also coinciding with Milken's event was the announcement of the inaugural 2027 cohort of the Elevate Investment Initiative. The effort, part of the Milken Institute’s Women Health Network, aims to mobilize $1 billion in net-new capital for women’s health innovation. The 10 fund managers and companies include Borski Fund, Cross-Border Impact Ventures, Foreground Capital, Meridian Health Ventures, How Women Invest and more. [cut this or move?].

Google Ads Quality Score is essentially a measurement of the quality and relevance of both your keywords and PPC ads. Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

For any industry, including real estate, a good Quality Score is generally around 7 or above. However, in the competitive world of real estate, striving for an even higher Quality Score could give you an advantage. So, for realtors, a great Quality Score might be considered 8 or above.

That said, keep in mind that a high-Quality Score is not an end in itself. It's a sign that your ads are relevant, and your landing pages provide a good user experience, but it's still just one factor in the overall success of your Google Ads campaigns.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The transition to full-time professional officials likely won't be completed by the start of the 2027 season.
  • "This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, unlike the typical ball sports, a significant number of on-track rule infractions are strictly tied to a specific penalty. The punishment is selected from a set range by part-time volunteers who are often criticized by drivers, teams and fans for their inconsistency. The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile confirmed on Thursday that it will be introducing full-time stewards to officiate Formula 1 next season. The sport's global governing body is finally shedding one of the last vestiges of its aristocratic past, aiming to provide more consistent rule calls. Welcome to 21st century, F1.

The transition to full-time professional officials likely won't be completed by the start of the 2027 season. The FIA stated it's establishing a department of 12 to 15 full-time stewards recruited from its existing pool of international stewards. While they will initially complement the current part-timers, the role of the permanent stewards will expand as their roster grows. Beyond officiating F1 race weekends, the full-timers will form a constant rule-decision base and train their eventual successors with those precedents. FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem said:.

"This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport. The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport.".

Sources indicate that formula 1 was formed in the same aristocratic primordial pool of international sports that encouraged the International Olympic Committee to ban professional athletes until 1986. European aristocrats held the reins of international motorsport until that same period. Prince Paul Alfons von Metternich-Winneburg finished a decade as FIA President in 1985. If the Metternich name sounds familiar, he was a great-grandson of Prince Klemens von Metternich, the influential 19th-century Austrian statesman.

Recent findings suggest that while F1 has become a multi-billion-dollar enterprise, the championship's officiating has long remained locked in an era when amateurism was a virtue. As a result, the F1 stewards' office is filled with people who can afford to spend significant time and money earning the prerequisite credentials and gaining the necessary experience officiating smaller events. The unpaid volunteers are often successful lawyers and automotive executives, sometimes employed by companies directly involved in F1. Thankfully, those days are finally coming to an end.
