📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that whelp, the AI boom has had one positive knock-on effect. It is creating newly introduced multi-millionaires by the bushel, any one of whom can afford to splurge on a pricey new electric vehicle. That aside, EV stakeholders in the US are springing back to life after a year-long slumber. Even General Motors is in play, stirring up long lost memories of its 1990’s-era EV1 debacle instead of hiding its head in shame. What’s up with that?

According to recent reports, I’m just going to stick my neck out and say that the eponymous Aptera solar-powered autocycle from the US startup Aptera will attract enough AI-enriched drivers to make a go of it. The on-again, off-again, on-again automaker has been on this year, working towards volume production of a plug-in, three-wheeled two-seater EV that can travel up to 40 miles on its own solar-plus-storage system (see more Aptera news here).

In a recent development, autocycles were once common here in the US and overseas markets, distinguished from motorcycles by their front-facing seats and steering wheels, rather than straddled seats and handlebars. They fell out of favor in the US by the middle of the 20th century, but 21st century hot-rodders have revived the form with a focus on eyebrow-raising, open-air, gas-guzzling showpieces. In particular, interest has spread in states that do not require autocycle drivers to invest in an additional motorcycle license.

It has been revealed that the Aptera is showy in its own right, resembling a rocket ship with unique aerodynamic styling. Perhaps it may even show up in the next James Bond adventure with James Pattinson at the wheel. In the meantime, the manufacturer has just made good on its pledge to reward early investors in the world’s first solar-powered car with the first production models to role off the assembly line. Aptera #1 goes to the founder and CEO of GDP Venture, Martin Hartono, aka “Accelerator #1.”.

Sources indicate that drivers can reserve an Aptera of their own for just $100, and they can expect to pay about $40,000 for the ride. Considering that the solar fuel is free, anyone in the mood for a head-turning ride will get quite a bargain for their $40,000 compared to other competitors in the zero emission two-seater field, such as the recently refreshed Tesla Roadster.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of refresh, General Motors has been weirdly lavishing attention on the EV1 sedan all this year, even though the automaker has been roundly criticized for the killing the short-lived car in its cradle. The automaker began producing EV1 electric sedans starting in 1996, following the unveiling of its Impact electric concept car in 1990. Unlike the Impact, EV1 was designed for use on the road. However, it was also designed mainly for the California market, and primarily for lease, not for sale. Production halted in 2003 at just about 1,000 vehicles, all to be recalled by GM and sent to the crusher as chronicled in Chris Paine’s 2006 documentary, “Who Killed The Electric Car?”.

Industry observers note that or, maybe not so weird after all. GM’s electrification journey long predates the launch of Tesla Motors in 2003. The legacy automaker is now determined to stake out its claim on automotive history, with 2026 marking the 30th anniversary of the start of EV1 production.

GM has been celebrating the anniversary all this year with multiple long form articles about the Impact and EV1 on its website, eager to remind everybody that its industry-leading vehicle electrification efforts of the 1990’s continue to manifest decades later, in the form of heat pumps for climate control, by-wire technology, and regenerative braking among other elements.

GM’s latest love letter to the EV1 popped up on November 17, when the automaker officially celebrated the completed restoration of the EV1 “V212” alongside its a private owner, Billy Caruso. The rare survivor of GM’s the junkyard crusher was evidently hiding out in an impound lot in Georgia all these years, until Caruso acquired it at auction and enlisted Jared Pink of the popular show The Questionable Garage to fix it up. Considering TQG’s large following on YouTube, GM wisely lent its engineers to the effort, along with several donated parts from its own EV1.

In a recent development, US President Donald Trump and the Republican majority in Congress have made a heroic effort to dial down the vehicle electrification movement, but facts on the ground keep getting in their way. For starters, today’s advanced batteries apply across multiple energy resources, fossil and non-fossil alike. So, it’s no surprise to see the US Department of Energy continuing to throw taxpayer dollars at newly introduced energy storage projects (here’s one example), even though some of that activity will eventually ripple into the vehicle electrification field.

The US Department of Defense is also getting into the act. DoD’s electrification journey has been a tedious one, but in recent years it has begun creeping stealthily towards a vision of ground mobility enabled by electricity, providing the key tactical advantages of silent running and a low heat signature.

Recent findings suggest that the latest news on that score involves a $1.4 billion loan commitment from DoD’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), enabling the silicon-based battery materials startup Sila to vault its signature product into commercial production. DoD’s primary interest in the company consists of applications in the electric drone and autonomous mobility fields, but Sila has long been eyeballing the EV market as well.

Sila secured the loan commitment in August, and it has not let the grass grow under its feet. On November 18 the manufacturer announced an off-take agreement with the well-known Tesla EV battery supplier Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America. “The multi-year agreement is part of a long-term commercial relationship with the potential for over $1 billion of offtake over time,” Sila explained in a press statement, further elaborating that Panasonic will deploy its proprietary Titan Silicon silicon-carbon anode material in battery cells.

Recent findings suggest that “The partnership is also expected to support significant manufacturing and construction job creation in the United States. With Sila’s U.S.-based anode production underpinned by proprietary American technology and know-how, Panasonic and its OEM customers gain a clearer path toward a more secure, resilient, and sustainable domestic supply chain,” Sila emphasized.

Industry observers note that that’s…interesting! Aside from Tesla as one of Sila’s OEM customers, keep an eye on another Panasonic offtaker, the up-and-comer US startup Harbinger Motors, which also has a foot in the DoD door.

The American Hospital Association (AHA) and West Health Institute declared Tuesday a latest collaboration with medtech company Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD) aimed at accelerating the adoption of technologies shown to improve patient care.

The collaboration builds on the West Health Accelerator at AHA’s Health Research & Educational Trust (HRET), a three-year initiative to aid healthcare organizations in scaling technology-enabled solutions.

It has been revealed that “No single organization can close the gap between innovation and everyday care on its own,” said Zia Agha, M.D., West Health Institute chief medical officer, in a statement. “This collaboration brings hospital reach, clinical technology expertise and performance intelligence together from the start. We’re beginning with a focused group of hospitals, learning what it takes to make changes last, and building a model that can reach hospitals of every size and resource level.”.

Recent findings suggest that the latest collaboration will begin with an initial cohort of 10 hospitals and health systems. It will incorporate advanced physiologic monitoring with clinical protocols in practice, specifically targeting complications associated with postoperative complications and longer hospital stays. Additionally, Vizient will provide performance benchmarking and analytic capabilities, the organizations stated.

Takeaways from the early cohort will help to identify adoption barriers, refine implementation approaches and outline necessary support to expand the model to a broader group.

BD Advanced Patient Monitoring Worldwide President Tim Patz said in a statement that the manufacturer believes innovation “has the greatest impact when it translates into meaningful improvements in patient care.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Our experience working with healthcare systems has shown us the value of bringing together advanced hemodynamic monitoring, data and the expertise of hospital care teams to support better-informed patient care,” Patz noted. “This collaboration gives us an opportunity to build on that experience, further integrate proven solutions into clinical practice and help more patients benefit from them.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Mercedes introduced the seventh-generation R232 SL roadster, it was only offered in performance-oriented AMG trims, with an ultra-luxury Maybach variant coming a few years later. For the first time in the model's history, a Benz-branded SL was missing from the lineup, but that's about to change because of buyer feedback. Some folks apparently miss the subdued, grand touring nature that SLs of old provided, and they don't all have the $230,000 it takes to enter Maybach land, so a Mercedes-Benz SL is coming back.

According to recent reports, with this current generation, Mercedes wanted to bring the SL and AMG GT Coupe closer together, and it seems that may have been a slight miscalculation on the German automaker's part. While substantial power and big prices are all well and good, it's not exactly what the average SL owner is looking for — especially when the Mercedes-AMG GT Coupe exists, according to Autocar. They missed some of the refinement and long-distance cruising ability of the old cars. Basically, the new one was hurting their agining backs.

It has been revealed that now that its mid-cycle refresh time, the GT will remain the performance-oriented vehicle, and the SL will take on a more relaxed demeaner, CEO Ola Källenius told Autocar. It'll trade in rock hard suspension and track times for comfort and ride quality. The two vehicles will also get revised engines to meet upcoming emissions standards in Communist Europe.

Mercedes will discontinue the entry-level SL43 and GT43 that use a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4, and the same fate will befall the SL63 S E Performance and its 805-horsepower plug-in-hybrid V8 powertrain. Instead, the updated SLs will all get 48-volt mild-hybrid systems, and the new entry-level engine is expected to be a 443-hp turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-6, which is far more befitting of a grand tourer anyway. That model will probably be called SL500, while an SL580 will have the new M177 Evo flat-plane crank V8 we first saw in the refreshed S-Class.

Don't worry, drop-top AMG fans. The AMG SL isn't going anywhere, even if the E Performance is. Autocar speculates that the M177 will be also used in an SL63 that'll put out a notch over 600 horsepower, which should be more than enough for the folks who are into things of that nature. (The AMG SL55 will effectively be replaced by the V8 Benz SL580.).

It's not just an ethos change, either. Mercedes states the Benz SL will have front-end styling that alighes closer with the standard Mercedes look, with a simpler grille that has one horizontal bar across it rather than the more aggressive AMG grille with all its vertical canes. It'll also make use of the latest Digital Light headlight system from the company, which, of course, features three-pointed-star daytime running lights. Inside, the car will get an upgraded MB.OS platform to run the infotainment and the rest of the car's brain as well as some fresh physical control.

Industry observers note that if this all sounds exciting to you in a way that the AMG SL didn't, well, you've got to hold on just a little bit longer. Källenius says the refreshed SL, which is going to be "more of a Mercedes-Benz," is expected to lauch in 2027.

#18933. Is AI A Public Or A Private Asset?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1105 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

Is AI A Public Or A Private Asset?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Isabelle Ferreras is a professor and research director at the University of Louvain, an Accelerator fellow at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford, and a senior research associate at the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard University.
  • In a recent development, she told The Guardian this week that she has grave concerns about the way AI and the corporations promoting it are managing this brave latest technology.
  • It has been revealed that last month, a person responsible for overseeing safety reports at OpenAI left the company, claiming its culture was “broken.” He added that the entire AI industry was careless when it comes to developing AI technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Isabelle Ferreras is a professor and research director at the University of Louvain, an Accelerator fellow at the Institute for Ethics in AI at the University of Oxford, and a senior research associate at the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard University. It safe to say she knows a thing or two about computer technology and AI.

In a recent development, she told The Guardian this week that she has grave concerns about the way AI and the corporations promoting it are managing this brave latest technology. Her concerns are spurred by the number of high profile computer engineers who have quit recently over fears that AI development is out of control.

It has been revealed that last month, a person responsible for overseeing safety reports at OpenAI left the company, claiming its culture was “broken.” He added that the entire AI industry was careless when it comes to developing AI technology. The month before that, a researcher at Anthropic — which went public yesterday at a valuation $1.8 trillion dollars — warned that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”.

Sources indicate that “When the only way for a conscientious engineer to raise the alarm is to leave,” Ferreras said. “it is a clear sign that corporate governance in the industry is broken. Each departure takes with it the very knowledge needed to steer these systems safely. We cannot regulate AI safely from the outside if the companies building it remain autocracies on the inside.”.

Ferreras warned that governments think of AI either as a “consumer product to be tested for defects or as a geopolitical race to be won by relaxing rules on business. Corporate lobbyists encourage this view as a trade-off between safety and innovation by arguing that legislation imposes too many burdens.

“This is a dangerous path. AI is not merely a software product. It is a technology of government. Yet inside frontier labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google, a handful of executives and capital investors decide which values are coded into models that shape millions of lives,” she mentioned.

Interestingly, Michael Connolly, the award winning author of the Bosch and Lincoln Lawyer novels, published a book last year in which the family of a young woman, who was murdered by her boyfriend after he interacted with an AI agent, sues the company behind the AI agent. The essence of the lawsuit is that AI only does what it is programmed to do, and since the lead programmer of this particular AI agent was a misogynist in real life, it reflected his values when it interacted with humans. The book is called The Proving Ground and it is a fascinating read.

In a recent development, while Ferreras applauds those who warn of the malignancies built into AI, she pointed out that humans have short attention spans. “Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. As a society, we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle — and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal. As the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.”.

In a democratic society, the exercise of governing power requires the consent of the governed, Ferreras told The Guardian. “Yet corporate law still treats firms as the property of shareholders, and the labor investors, who put their intellect, health and lives into the firm, as subordinates. To align AI with the public interest, we need a dual strategy: alongside solid public regulations on AI ‘from the outside,’ we need to enter the corporate black box and force corporate governance into alignment with democratic principles.”.

An analogy can be made to the Federal Communications Commission, which licenses broadcasters and promotes the free flow of information to the public. The digital world thinks such controls are archaic, but the lack of them is a clear and present danger to a civil society.

Ferreras suggested that “governments must outlaw non-disclosure and non-disparagement clauses that silence staff on safety risks, and enact robust whistle blower protection. Tech workers also need a collective standing over corporate strategy, independent channels to report safety breaches, and formal representation inside frontier labs before models are deployed.”.

In addition, she argued that “legislators must establish a binding right to co-decision over workplace AI. No algorithmic system that monitors, evaluates or disciplines workers should be deployed without prior negotiation. At national and EU level, we need to consider collective bargaining on AI deployment and veto rights for works councils or trade unions, backed by independent technical experts and a strict ban on automated firing.”.

It has been revealed that lastly, she supported the democratization of boardrooms and rewarding firms that refuse to concentrate power at the top. “Legislators should mandate worker-elected directors on boards, moving towards dual-majority governance in which strategic decisions require the consent not only of capital but of labor.” Some, like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, would characterize her suggestions as liberal claptrap, and they would be correct. Ferreras would happily unravel the “tech bro” manosphere in order to promote a more open and just society.

According to recent reports, she pointed to the research by Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson, the 2024 Nobel laureates in economics, which demonstrates that technological revolutions do not automatically produce shared prosperity. Instead, institutions decide who benefits and who pays.

“Extending democracy into the firm is not an old battle over power for its own sake, but a practical necessity for more ethical judgment. Aligning AI with the good of workers and society requires more wisdom than closed executive rooms can offer. It needs what the Yale political theorist Hélène Landemore calls ‘democratic reason’ — the collective intelligence of diverse, deliberating voices, brought to bear on corporate decision-making,” Ferreras wrote.

“Left to self-regulation and the occasional whistleblower, AI governance will entrench an unaccountable algorithmic oligarchy. Accountability and alignment begins with giving those who build these systems and those whose work they govern an enforceable voice, from the code floor to the boardroom.”.

It has been revealed that ferreras’ point of view is decidedly liberal, and yet her arguments are clear and concise. How can we give so much power to digital agents and not take reasonable steps to ensure the needs of society as a whole are respected? The tech industry enjoys almost unfettered freedom of action today. It may be time to consider whether that is a good long term strategy.

Payer mix, non-labor expenses dragged hospital margins in September" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hospitals’ operations took another dip in September amid a slew of ongoing headwinds including weakened payer mix and rising costs, healthcare advisory firm Kaufman Hall reported alongside warnings of a “historically large portion” of the nation’s hospitals running on negative or near-zero operating margins.

The firm’s latest monthly benchmark report, released Tuesday, showed a calendar year-to-date operating margin index of 1.4% and a single-month operating margin index of 2.4% in September, the latter of which was a decline from August’s 3.0% operating margin (all including health system allocations for shared services costs).

In a recent development, the performance decline wasn’t for want of patients. Daily discharges and adjusted discharges both rose 3% from August to September, and are generally above the numbers from last year. Operating room minutes per calendar day also rose 6% from August—an encouraging sign for hospitals whose surgical slowdowns had hamstrung acuity—but remain 1% below September of last year.

The increased foot traffic also grew revenues, with daily net operating revenue rising 4% from August and 6% year over year while gross operating revenue rose 4% month to month and 8% year over year. Much of the increase came on the outpatient side, where daily revenue increased 5% from August and 10% compared to September 2025. Net patient service revenue per adjusted discharge was more mixed, rising 2% from August but remaining 1% below September 2025.

However, hospitals’ margins are being challenged by persistent bad debt and charity care burdens, Kaufman Hall’s data show. Daily bad debt and charity care may have remained flat from August, but is 17% higher than September 2025 and 16% higher when comparing both years’ first nine months. As a percentage of gross operating revenue, they’re 6% higher than Sept. 2025 and 8% higher year to date.

Sources indicate that on the spending side, daily total expense rose 3% from August and is 5% higher than September 2025, primarily reflecting the heightened volumes even as hospitals held their average length of stay flat month over month or 1% shorter year over year. The expenses were more pronounced on the non-labor side, where increases on a per adjusted discharge basis were higher than labor’s per adjusted discharge decline.

Sources indicate that "Hospitals continue to operate in an environment marked by significant financial variability," Erik Swanson, managing director and Data and Analytics group leader at Kaufman Hall, stated in a release. “Many organizations continue to face mounting pressure from uncompensated care and rising expenses, underscoring the importance of proactive operational and financial strategies that build long-term resilience.".

Another amplifying market trend is the “bifurcation of hospital performance” often highlighted by the firm and others that monitor multi-organization financial trends, such as credit rating agencies.

According to recent reports, "The margin gap between higher and lower-performing hospitals has widened to 19 percentage points, with a historically large portion of hospitals operating at negative or very thin margins,” the report reads. “Even slight revenue reductions threaten organizations, which face increasingly difficult decisions on future operations, care delivery, and expense control.”.

The firm encouraged hospitals to take “deliberate, proactive steps” to strengthen their financial situations, particularly as macro reimbursement trends stiffen and the site of care delivery shifts from the hospital to outpatient settings.

Kaufman Hall’s hospital reports pull data from more than 1,300 nationwide hospitals as collected by parent manufacturer Strata Decision Technology.

Accompanying the monthly hospital benchmark was also Kaufman Hall’s quarterly numbers on more than 200,000 employed physicians and advanced practice providers, which painted a much rosier picture for health system and hospital employers.

It showed, for the first time in five years of data collection, that healthcare employers’ investment/subsidy per provider and per physician has declined year over year (by 1%), and “across every cohort, including primary care, medical specialty, surgical specialty and hospital-based specialty.”.

Kaufman Hall attributed the rare turnaround to revenue growth and sustained productivity increases that together outpaced expenses.

According to recent reports, "Medical groups made meaningful performance improvements this quarter, achieving gains in revenue, productivity and thoughtful workforce management," Matthew Bates, managing director and Physician Enterprise Service Line leader at Kaufman Hall, remarked in a release. "The growing utilization of [advanced practice providers] and ongoing focus on operational and team effectiveness are helping organizations manage financial pressures while increasing access to care.”.

#18928. The Metals Organization Has a Seabed Mining Production Gap That Its Pilot Has Not Closed

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1076 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

The Metals Organization Has a Seabed Mining Production Gap That Its Pilot Has Not Closed

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1076 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2022, The Metals Organization (TMC) and offshore contractor Allseas recovered 3,021 wet tons of nodules from the Pacific seabed.
  • In a recent development, what matters between those endpoints is the operating record: sustained collection rates, marine maintenance, vessel availability and delivered tons sufficient to carry fixed costs.
  • The November 12, 2026 corporate update describes a phased approach: begin with an upgraded pilot collector and limited modifications to Hidden Gem, then invest in larger systems as operations develop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2022, The Metals Organization (TMC) and offshore contractor Allseas recovered 3,021 wet tons of nodules from the Pacific seabed. Their integrated test system moved material up a riser stretching more than four kilometres from the ocean floor to the Hidden Gem. During production runs, the collector achieved 86.4 wet tons per hour. Four years later, TMC is discussing a million tons a year from an upgraded system and eventually 12 million tons annually across four vessels.

In a recent development, what matters between those endpoints is the operating record: sustained collection rates, marine maintenance, vessel availability and delivered tons sufficient to carry fixed costs. TMC has yet to demonstrate those economics.

The November 12, 2026 corporate update describes a phased approach: begin with an upgraded pilot collector and limited modifications to Hidden Gem, then invest in larger systems as operations develop. Phasing reduces the initial capital commitment. It also pushes the demonstration of the projected commercial production rates into the future.

In a recent development, the annual arithmetic is straightforward. At 5,000 productive hours, about 57% of a calendar year, a system collecting 200 wet tons per hour delivers one million tons. The second-year target of 1.5 million tons requires 300 tons per hour. Three million tons from one production system requires 600 tons per hour. TMC’s 2022 production-run rate of 86.4 tons per hour would deliver 432,000 tons at that utilization.

The upgraded machines are expected to be different from the 2022 test collector. Their performance must be demonstrated, not assumed from the pilot. The operating gap is central to the project economics, and it grows with production ambitions.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing examines TMC’s production gap alongside Impossible Metals’ autonomous collection model and the investment consequences of underperforming equipment. The source assessment and fleet sensitivities are linked there.

Industry observers note that A collector, a multi-kilometre hydraulic riser and a production vessel have to work together. The crawler encounters uneven ground and varying nodule coverage. The riser and pumps handle abrasive slurry. The vessel must remain on station while crews inspect, maintain and repair equipment. Offshore access and weather affect when those activities can occur.

A system can produce at its test rate and still lose the year on maintenance and interruptions. Fewer productive hours push the required hourly rate higher. Repeating a successful short production run does not establish a year’s availability, let alone multiple years of fleet productivity.

The difference matters because capital and offshore operating costs continue while production is interrupted. Ships, crews, marine maintenance equipment and financing cost money whether or not nodules are arriving on deck. Smaller annual production spreads fixed expenses over fewer tons and raises the cost of every ton recovered.

Sources indicate that TMC’s August 2025 prefeasibility presentation estimated offshore collection and transport at $179 per dry ton, or about $129 per wet ton under its 28% moisture assumption. Those are projections for a future system. They are not an audited cost record from continuous industrial mining. The revised first-production configuration needs its own cost data.

The missing commercial evidence is a long enough operating record to estimate productive hours, rate degradation, planned and unplanned maintenance, retrieval time, replacement costs and the delivered cost per ton. Until then, moving from a pilot to a production forecast remains a major assumption.

In a recent development, impossible Metals proposes to collect individual nodules with autonomous underwater vehicles rather than a tracked crawler and riser. A vehicle would descend, select nodules, fill its cargo compartment, return, undergo surface recovery, unload and prepare for another mission. Every trip must be repeated across an entire fleet.

In a recent development, its September 2026 scientific trial, reported by Reuters, recovered approximately 450 grams of nodules from more than 4,000 metres depth. It demonstrated selective scientific collection. A commercial robot would have to carry vastly more material and sustain cycle times and availability that the experiment did not measure.

In a recent development, in the 2025 commercial concept examined by metallurgical specialist Lyle Trytten and me, each proposed vehicle carried 12 tons of nodules and had 18 collection arms. At one nodule every 1.5 seconds per arm and an average nodule mass of 100 grams, filling the cargo requires roughly 120,000 successful picks. With all arms continuously working, collection alone occupies approximately 2.8 hours.

The proposed complete mission cycle was four hours. Descent, ascent, searching, repositioning, failed picks, recovery, unloading, inspection and relaunch also consume time. The architecture has too many interdependent activities to fit those requirements into that cycle at the assumed performance.

According to recent reports, autonomous navigation and manipulator tests cannot substitute for evidence of an entire fleet repeatedly executing commercial missions. Increasing payload changes vehicle weight, buoyancy, energy use and recovery equipment. Faster picking leaves the surface operation and deepwater transit to be solved.

Recent findings suggest that our 2025 independent techno-economic assessment tested the financial effects of weaker-than-assumed robot productivity. At the illustrative $180 per dry ton nodule sales value, the model required approximately $2.52 billion in capital with the originally assumed robot throughput. Halving throughput while maintaining output increased required capital to approximately $4.51 billion.

At a 10% discount rate, the modeled net present value moved from positive $863 million to negative $769 million. Even at two-thirds of original productivity, NPV fell to about $15 million, a negligible margin for a multibillion-dollar first-of-a-kind industrial fleet.

Sources indicate that these are scenario calculations, not actual bills or calibrated probabilities. They identify the key failure mode: more robots, recovery capacity, batteries, vessels and maintenance are needed to compensate for each production shortfall. A financial model based on high productivity can look attractive until realistic availability and turnaround times are included.

In a recent development, TMC is further along technologically than Impossible Metals, but its future-scale production economics are also unsupported by a sustained operating record. Neither tech giant has demonstrated the productive hours, throughput and maintenance costs needed to support its advertised commercial proposition.

It has been revealed that policymakers and investors should ask for extended end-to-end offshore operating records and audited unit economics before treating future production targets as investable output. The technology risk exists before accounting for nodule processing, metals markets, permitting or environmental liabilities.

It has been revealed that the complete TFIE Briefing and linked assessment show the fleet calculations, technical assumptions and capital sensitivities. The remaining articles in the five-part series address processing, metals markets and American Samoa’s exposure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Friends, I'm going to give you a little peek behind the curtain at how this, your most beloved weekly automotive column, works. It goes like this: I find a bunch of car listings, and then I write a couple thousand words about them. You might expect the former to be the fun part, browsing all week for newly introduced and interesting listings, but it's actually the back half I really enjoy. See, finding listings has a problem: Eventually, things get old.

That's why you need gimmicks. Cars from a certain area, cars with a certain theme, cars from history's greatest cinematic achievement. Today, the gimmick is price: A hard cap of $5,000, which no vehicle exceeds. I honestly expected a bunch of beige commuter cars in questionable stated of repair, but I'm shocked at how good the offerings were in rust-free states. We've got Benzes, BMWs, and bikes as far as the eye can see. Welcome, my friends, to a budget-conscious edition of the week's Dopest Cars.

According to recent reports, remember when nice FR-Ses or BRZs cost five figures? Well, they still do. This example is no one's definition of immaculate, but it should be everyone's definition of a deal. This is Miata money! Less than Miata money! For under five grand, you could have one of the best-handling chassis out there, and with an engine that's not even blown! Yet. Probably.

Even if/when that does happen, $5,000 leaves plenty of room in the budget for something new to go under that theoretically carbon hood. K-swap, 2JZ, RB26, LS, EJ257, everything fits. Do whatever you want forever with this car, because it's up for whatever. You can fit anything between those front wheels, and you should. Do something cool with it, then reach out to me and send me pictures and videos of the cool thing you did. I'll write about it. That's an Amber promise. (Amber does not get to make these promises. -Ed).

According to recent reports, not only is there a upcoming liquid-cooled replacement for this old 411cc Himalayan out there, in the form of the Himalayan 450, but there's now a bigger brother in Enfield's adventure lineup with the Himi 750. This is neither of those, but they're still relevant here because their very existence makes the first-generation Himalayan cheaper by comparison. It's slower, less powerful, and altogether not as advanced a bike — perfect for those of you looking to get started with something approachable.

In a recent development, personally, I see the appeal in a dead-simply little ADV like the Himalayan 411. There's so little to go wrong, it's the kind of adventure bike that you can actually really adventure with. Sure, service intervals aren't Honda long, but good luck getting an Africa Twin for three grand. The Himalayan won't get you anywhere fast, it won't be the most stylish way around, but it'll certainly get you where you're going.

Yeah, I was surprised too. A Z32 300ZX, in seemingly good shape, for under $5,000. Are cars just free in the states where they don't rust away into dust after two winters? Do you Arizonans just have your pick of any cool car you want for approximately the price of a Costco hot dog? Don't tell me. I can't bear to know.

Recent findings suggest that anyway, this 300ZX isn't perfect, so at least I can take some solace in that while I scroll my locally-available rustbuckets and cry myself to sleep. It needs a whole wheel bearing, something that's surely a pain to replace on a completely rust-free car where none of the undercarriage bolts have fused to each other and become one piece of metal that's inseparable no matter how much heat and torque you apply. Surely that's the case. Please just let me have this one. Not even this car, just this dream of perfect-car availability outside my region.

Recent findings suggest that pink R6! Well, pinkish gray. It's pinker than any factory fairings for the bike, at least. Actually, none of you are allowed to buy this one, I want it for myself once I win a quick Powerball. Just keep scrolling to the next slide.

Mister Two? More like mister too expensive, except in Southern California where these can apparently be had for $4,500. I see why so many car and bike people live there, with the beautiful roads and temperate climate and availability of cars that aren't just piled of rust with a VIN. I get the appeal, but unfortunately I can never join you all. If I spend more than five days in LA I start to go mad due to lack of walkable infrastructure.

Anyway, MR2. This one's not a turbo car, but that doesn't really matter for this kind of money. It also has a beat-up body kit, but again I don't really care. In fact, I prefer a car that has a couple dents, dings, and battle scars — it wears its story on its body panels. This isn't a garage queen, it's a car that's really been used the way its engineers and designers intended. That's worth celebrating, and each rock scratch and bit of drift stitching is a celebration in itself.

According to recent reports, are people over 240Ds now? Have they all moved on to J80 Land Cruisers or something? Back in my day, a 240D in this kind of condition for this kind of money would barely last a day on Marketplace or Craigslist, let alone the weeks this one's been on the market. I know, it's not a wagon, but still. It's not gasoline either!

Recent findings suggest that the seller of this particular 240 claims that it not only runs and drives, but has a fairly considerable amount of work done under the hood. The battery, starter, glow plugs, injectors, and fluids are all new. There's also some unspecified "work" on the head, which probably doesn't mean it's been overheated and warped at some point in its history. I'd bet that didn't happen. How would you even overheat a dependable old Volvo diesel like that, even if you wanted to? These things are so bulletproof.

Not every sub-$5,000 car on Facebook Marketplace is an enthusiast icon. I accept that. That doesn't mean that the remainder have to be bad, though — they can be beloved commuter cars with more sporting pretensions than they really need, like this Mazda3. It's no MazdaSpeed, sure, but it's a stick-shift compact sedan with Mazda's jinba ittai philosophy behind its chassis, engine, and suspension design. I think that's pretty good.

Industry observers note that this one seems to be in good shape, and the seller certainly claims the same, though it's a little tough to tell what exactly is going on in the photos. They're so smudged, or blurry, or streaked with sun — I can't even tell why they're wrong, I just know that they are. It's still a good car, but damn, Marketplace sellers. Step your photography game up. Or, at least, wipe your phone camera on your shirt before you take your listing photos.

There's been a Prelude parked outside my girlfriend's apartment for a few weeks now, and it looks a lot like this one. Red, not white, but in a similar state of aged-yet-solid — not the cleanest, not the stock-est, but still more than drivable. Well, I assume it's drivable, but it hasn't moved for street sweeping in a while. I hope it's drivable.

According to recent reports, this Prelude not only drives, but ought to drive pretty well — it's an Si model, after all. The seller states it's "mechanically pristine" but that the interior needs work, though it looks perfect inside and out to my eye. Maybe I just have lower standards for my car interiors, but this one looks great. All I can see is a bit of work heeded on the sunroof shade, and what might be the tiniest rip in the side of the driver's seat. I don't think either of those are worth addressing with anything more than a bit of gaffer's tape, honestly.

Recent findings suggest that hey, it's my old bike! Not exactly, mine was a better color, but I did ride a G 310 GS when I first moved to Latest York and started working at the good ship Jalopnik. I maintain that a baby ADV is secretly the best way to get started on two wheels, provided you're tall enough to manage the seat height —  they can do a bit of everything, and they'll help you figure out where you want to spend your two-wheel time. Try it all on a small adventure bike, then see what you like doing best and cater your next bike towards that.

It has been revealed that this particular G 310 GS, though, has one benefit over mine: It's much cheaper. I sold mine for something like $6,000, and this one's asking just $4,000 — surely you can talk the seller down from that. Imagine picking this bike up for a cool $3,500! You'd have a fantastic beginner bike. I got almost too comfortable on mine, riding it sidesaddle and one-legged through Brooklyn traffic, and you could get that same level of comfort on two wheels.

C'mon, I don't need to sell you on this one. A Suzuki Sidekick for under $2,000! Just go buy it.

Industry observers note that the digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was rolled out in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it notes. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to users, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup.

Schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

DJ and music producer Steve Aoki told the HLTH audience that his father's passing was the catalyst for his interest in healthcare.

It’s been several weeks since Doximity integrated Wolters Kluwer Health’s UpToDate into its AI clinical decision support tool.

Doximity VP of Clinical AI Partnerships Kamal Menghrajani, M.D., told Fierce Healthcare at HLTH said the integration gives her “a little bit more confidence” in her own practice.

“Now I can use UpToDate to supplement and feel like what I'm doing at the point of care really is the best thing for the patient,” she remarked.

Menghrajani, who previously served as assistant director for cancer innovation and public health at the White House, took on the role with Doximity approximately four months ago.

Industry observers note that “[I get to] be the physician voice and represent the interests of doctors within the company,” she stated. “And think about what it looks like to actually take the tools we're building and serve doctors better.”.

Sources indicate that menghrajani stated the rapid expansion of the tech giant’s AI suite has been a key takeaway, adding that a focus for the company is what physicians want out of AI. “I've seen Doximity evolve to meet all of those needs,” Menghrajani said.

As a range of AI tools saturate the industry, Menghrajani said the biggest use she has seen amongst clinicians is ambient scribes. “I think that has been a real game changer in terms of actual practice,” she said.

On the HLTH show floor, you may have noticed a theme.

Las Vegas is abuzz with the upcoming Formula 1 race, which is taking place on Saturday, Nov. 21. The city has been preparing for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, which is on the Strip, for weeks, and HLTH is taking place at one of the hubs for F1 excitement, The Venetian.

According to recent reports, so at this year's conference, each of the stages is themed around racing: the Velocity Stage, the Ferrari Stage, the Monacco Stage. And each breakout track is referred to as a "circuit." In the conference livery, HLTH mascot Petunia is show driving a race car.

Activations on the show floor also play into the F1 theme. A racing simulation game is set up for attendees near the Pharma Force stage, and swag giveaways allude to the race.

Panelists at a HLTH session discussing the uptake of ICHRA — scratch that, CHOICE — faced a challenge around the nomenclature.

Individual coverage health reimbursement arrangements, or ICHRAs, represent a growing area of interest for employers and insurers participating in the individual market. But on Sept. 3, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that it would instead refer to these models as CHOICE, which stands for Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense.

In a recent development, in these models, an employer offers enrollees a stipend to purchase coverage on the individual market rather than securing a traditional employer-sponsored strategy. ICHRA (or CHOICE) has gained traction with employers that may otherwise struggle to offer health coverage.

Recent findings suggest that moderator Joseph Mercer, senior managing director at Marwood Group, joked that the panelists had all agreed to call these prepares CHOICE rather than ICHRA. But throughout the session, slip-ups drew a chuckle.

Even the panel's title made reference to the evolution of the name: "The ICHRA (CHOICE) Debate.".

Healthcare platform Simple HealthKit confirmed Tuesday a partnership with Waters Corporation to expand access to at-home cervical cancer screening.

The collaboration aims to expand access to BD’s Onclarity HPV Self-Collection Kit, which is tested with the BD Onclarity HPV Assay  and Simple HealthKit's artificial intelligence-powered direct-to-patient-provider platform.

Sources indicate that "We envision a future where personalized, world-class healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of where they live,” remarked Sheena Menezes, Ph.D, Simple HealthKit CEO and co-founder, in a statement. “Our AI-powered direct-to-patient and provider platform brings that vision to life by connecting people with the right education, intelligent personalized engagement, and clinical care at every step.”.

Menezes continued, “Through partnerships with innovators like Waters Corporation, we are empowering individuals to take charge of their health while making seamless, personalized care accessible at scale.”.

Oura CEO joined Counsel Health CEO and founder Muthu Alagappan Tuesday morning to discuss the wearable firm’s recently unveiled $625 million acquisition of the virtual primary care company.

Hale said Oura selected Counsel as a partner after reviewing the landscape, and “uptake” from customers was “very positive.”.

Industry observers note that “We started talking seriously about taking that partnership,” Hale said. “And while we had been dating for a while, we thought maybe it was time to get married.”.

Hale said the agreement was “really driven” by Oura customers using Counsel in “really novel and interesting ways.”.

Alagappan remarked one of the most exciting aspects of the partnership is the potential impact of AI-fueled access to physicians on preventive care, adding the daily engagement of wearing Oura rings struck him.

“The buy-in from almost all people is tremendous, and so you enable primary care with the thing that has always been missing, which is engagement,” he stated. “And now we have a way to incentivize, motivate patients to make the changes that actually prevent disease, alongside the screenings and lab tests that are also very important.”.

During a Monday fireside chat, CMS Deputy Administrator and Chief Product Officer Amy Gleason remarked HHS and OCR colleagues “have done an amazing job” at looking at the issue to “remove friction from the patient experience.”.

It has been revealed that gleason remarked there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a “personal health app,” identity verification and speed. “It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also says that this information is free to the patient,” she said.

Throughout the session with Zus Health CEO and co-founder Jonathan Bush, Gleason also touted the agency’s voluntary CMS Health Tech Ecosystem initiative.

In a recent development, “The idea of this was to stop waiting on regulation, like healthcare does for some reason, and to just charge forward and get the technology and people that are willing to go faster to work on it,” Gleason remarked. “And we set up a bunch of different technology working groups that are really about taking the friction out of the system.”.

Evvy CEO and co-founder Priyanka Jain spoke with Fierce Healthcare Monday about research gaps in women’s health and how her tech giant looks to bridge them through vaginal microbiome testing.

Jain said women were excluded from medical research from 1977 to 1993 after a drug being prescribed off-label for morning sickness was causing birth defects, adding the ramifications ar still being seen today.

According to recent reports, “Women to this day are diagnosed on average four years later than men across over 700 diseases,” Jain stated. “And it's hard to not point right back to the fact that we didn't study women until 1993.”.

According to recent reports, to bridge these gaps, Evvy offers an at-home vaginal health test with clinician-reviewed results and personalized treatment plans. “If we've essentially never studied women, then there must be so many biomarkers in the female body that we under leverage in our definition of health and disease, and so that's our focus,” Jain stated.

Jain added Evvy uses AI and precision medicine to “actually predict the right treatment programs” for each patient using the biomarkers.

And, Jain said women’s health needs attention, awareness and funding when asked about recent Trump administration initiatives to focus on women’s health.

According to recent reports, “I’m really excited to see the attention and awareness that has been happening,” Jain noted. “But now we need to actually move dollars.”.

Department of Health and Human Services Chief Counselor Chris Klomp remarked the administration is focused on bringing in top tech talent as it looks to make the massive, but aging, government insurance system work better.

Klomp spoke on a panel Monday morning at HLTH, where he discussed the challenges in harvesting the data necessary to transform Medicare, Medicaid and other key government programs. Klomp was recently nominated to serve as Deputy Secretary at HHS and is a rising star in the White House.

He said that technology can play a critical role in accelerate processes that have been historically inefficient and time consuming. At the Food and Drug Administration, for example, tech is hastening the process of developing drugs and making approvals, a timeline that previously taken a decade or more.

But embracing technology in this way isn't compromising safety for these medications, Klomp stated.

In addition, he noted the administration is leaning on the personal nature of healthcare to bring in workers with the tech know-how necessary to drive critical advancements and change.

"Most people don't care about healthcare unless you work in it," he remarked. "People also start to care about healthcare when you lose your health, or someone you love loses their health. And than it swiftly becomes the most important thing to you.".

"We're using that as an opportunity to drive requirement, drive amazing talent," Klomp mentioned.

Houston Methodist unveiled Monday it has expanded its advanced inpatient monitoring care to include rural hospitals throughout Kansas.

Participating hospitals will provide patients with Medtronic’s BioButton, which continuously monitors vital signs, while the Houston Methodist remote monitoring team will review the data and work with bedside nurses.

It has been revealed that the vital monitoring devices are used at all eight acute-care hospitals in the Houston Methodist system, across more than 2,500 inpatient beds, according to the Nov. 11 announcement.

“Innovation is most meaningful when we identify patient needs, take what works or doesn't work and find newly introduced ways to extend the positive impact,” said Sara Loewy, Houston Methodist virtual care vice president, in a statement. “What we’ve built in Houston has the potential to reach much further. By thoughtfully extending this model into new care settings, our goal with this program is to demonstrate how our system’s existing technology and clinical expertise can strengthen access and improve outcomes in rural communities.”.

Loewy added the expansion is an opportunity to “explore how the capabilities of a major health system can be shared across geographic boundaries.”.

While 72% of health tech startups lead with “AI-powered” in their descriptors, zero surveyed venture capitalists in a newly introduced report from HLTH and SolComms remarked the phrase increased their confidence.

Independently surveyed health tech reporters also ranked “AI-powered” as one of the most overused phrases in pitching–in addition to “revolutionizing/transforming” and “disrupting.”.

Alongside these survey responses, researchers compared–and scored–the messaging of 72 U.S.-based, venture-backed health tech startups at series A to series C for the “Healthtech Attention Economy Report.” Startups’ messaging across their website and social media was scored on four main dimensions: clarity, differentiation, proof and policy awareness.

SolComms Vice President of HealthTech Isabella Morreale said in a statement the companies that will get attention within the next year “are leading with proof, not adjectives.”.

“That means speaking to clinical data, measurable outcomes, and validation from third parties,” Morreale said. “Founder-led storytelling will also continue to stand out. Among the data, one common through-thread for investor and reporter interest was founders with a real point of view on the industry.”.

Morreale continued, “Reporters don't need another tech giant description; they need a source who can help them explain what's happening in healthcare.”.

Less than half (42.2%) of patients say communications from healthcare providers “often” or “always” feel relevant to their needs, a latest report from Lirio found.

Sources indicate that analysts at the behavioral science and AI-powered behavioral intelligence platform polled 1,500 adults across the U.S. for the survey. While 58% of respondents report communications not consistently feeling relevant to their needs, 55.6% rate overall communication experiences with healthcare organizations as “good” or “excellent.”.

When asked why healthcare communications are ignored altogether, respondents report generic or irrelevant content (24.4%), too many similar messages (21.8%) and confusing, jargon-filled messages (18.8%) as top reasons.

Nearly half of respondents (47.9%) report the potential value of more personalized, better-timed messages as an “8, 9 or 10” for how much it could help them make better care decisions and stay engaged.

Lirio Chief Behavioral Officer Amy Bucher, Ph.D., remarked in a statement patients “are not rejecting healthcare communications outright.”.

In a recent development, “They are telling us, in specific and measurable terms, that the system is talking at them instead of to them,” Bucher remarked. "The instinct in healthcare has long been to solve engagement with more outreach - more emails, more reminders, more portals. This data shows that volume is not the problem. What is missing is relevance — content and timing designed for where a specific patient is in their own health journey, rather than a single message broadcast to an entire population.”.

Bucher added the healthcare organizations that close the communication gap will be “the ones that use behavioral data to determine the right message, the right channel, and the right moment for each individual patient, which is the model Lirio was built to deliver.".

Community-based specialty palliative care provider Vynca is expanding its reach into four more states.

Patients will now be able to access Vynca’s services in Georgia, Hawaii, Newly introduced Jersey and Texas. Vynca is one of the first practices approved to provide services under New Jersey’s Community-Based Palliative Care Medicaid benefit, launched in April, according to the Nov. 16 announcement.

Founded in 2013, the company’s hybrid care model combines in-home visits with virtual clinical support and predictive technology, and executives say it has shown 43% fewer emergency department visits and 52% less hospital stays within six months of enrollment.

“Health plan and government program leaders understand the value of community-based palliative care for people with serious illness,” said Darren Schulte, M.D., Vynca CEO, in a statement. “Our expansion in four key states reflects growing momentum to expand specialty outpatient palliative care outside of hospices. The key is to broaden access and convenience for the entire eligible population by offering home-based options. Too often, patients are limited to seeking palliative care when available in the community, at hospital-based clinics and facilities.”.

AI’s next build-out: Inference racks that resize themselves for every newly introduced model

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Memory pooling is fast becoming one of the sharpest tools in AI inference economics, with companies racing to wring more output from every graphics processing unit.
  • Most AI servers still ship with a fixed GPU-to-memory ratio that holds for the life of the machine.
  • “Our core fundamental technology is around pooling and sharing the most critical resources in the data center, which are now GPU and memory,” Puri remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:43 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Memory pooling is fast becoming one of the sharpest tools in AI inference economics, with companies racing to wring more output from every graphics processing unit.

Most AI servers still ship with a fixed GPU-to-memory ratio that holds for the life of the machine. But that is a poor fit when nobody knows what model they will deploy six months from now, according to Sumit Puri (pictured), co-founder and chief technical officer of Liqid Inc.

“Our core fundamental technology is around pooling and sharing the most critical resources in the data center, which are now GPU and memory,” Puri remarked. “Rather than statically deploying these things inside of a server, our vision is simple. Let’s put pools of resources in the rack, GPUs and memory, and dynamically assign them to any server that needs it based upon the model or the workload that we are looking to deploy.”.

Puri spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed pooling GPUs and memory, the tokenomics of AI inference and Liqid as a Service. (* Disclosure below.).

Liqid measures payoff in tokenomics, with the yardsticks being tokens per second, tokens per watt and, above all, tokens per dollar. Supply is another pressure point in the AI infrastructure build-out, with memory among its most constrained components. But delivering only the memory each application needs stretches scarce supply further, Puri explained.

Industry observers note that “Supply chain is a massive constraint for all of us — memory being a giantly massive constrained thing,” he noted. “If we can do things like pool memory, share memory, optimally deliver memory to the server in the right amount of memory as required by the application, we can directly address some of those supply chain complications.”.

In a recent development, liqid is also widening how customers buy memory pooling. At SC26, the organization unveiled Liqid as a Service, a fully managed, single-tenant offering, and it is moving toward preconfigured appliances. The bet is that most enterprises will deploy models rather than build them and therefore require their own capacity, according to Puri.

“The world went to unlimited consumption of minutes, and that’s where we believe tokens are headed,” Puri mentioned. “Everybody’s going to own their own token machine so they can consume these tokens at will.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We took a trip to see the Kia PV5 electric van.
  • Inspired by a comment in the Electric Vehicle Council report about electric vans, Majella and I decided to have a short visit to a group of dealerships under the Norris Motors banner.
  • Julie Delvecchio, the CEO of EVC, calls the lack of affordable electric vans in Australia “the single biggest unclaimed opportunity left.” We think that is about to change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We took a trip to see the Kia PV5 electric van. Our brief takeaway: “Kool like a Kia.” Should keep the bean counters happy.

Inspired by a comment in the Electric Vehicle Council report about electric vans, Majella and I decided to have a short visit to a group of dealerships under the Norris Motors banner. We hoped to check out the LDV eDeliver 5 van, touted as selling for under AU$50,000. However, there was no stock to view and we ended up chatting to the dealer and then moving on to the MG U9 BEV ute. You can read about it here. And then we found the Kia PV5 delivery van.

Julie Delvecchio, the CEO of EVC, calls the lack of affordable electric vans in Australia “the single biggest unclaimed opportunity left.” We think that is about to change. Since its launch in May, 496 PV5 have sold in Australia.

The Kia PV5 reminded me a lot of the Renault Kangoo in both size and shape, and it is able to carry about the same payload. And the front looked like the BMW i3. The one we looked at had been sold and was awaiting a fitout as a camper van. The Norris Group Kia specialist was generous with his time and the information he shared. He has been selling the Kia EV5 for the past 5 months and delivered 5 of the vans. He sold his first one within a week of its arrival on the lot — to Ray, a driver working for Amazon.

Ray appreciated the 390 km range. My friendly sales rep tells me that this will be increased in 2027 models to 420 km. Ray was getting out of diesel and most of his questions were around charging and regen braking. Most of his trips were around the burbs and he was not intending to take the van on the highway. The Kia PV5 is a workhorse, with a passenger car feel and level of comfort. It even has electric lumbar support for the driver — great when you are spending so much time in the van delivering parcels in the lead-up to Christmas. It certainly has a lot more tech than the diesel he was trading in.

It has been revealed that in fact, he was “blown away” by the standard features — the 360-degree camera, for example. “Vans are not known for their visibility.” On his return to the dealership for his first service, he commented on the smoothness of the torque: “It has no problems going uphill.” He reported that the van felt “well planted on the road.” Ray has gotten used to trickle charging at home and has lost his range anxiety. Like most fresh EV drivers, once he started living and working with the vehicle, his fears vanished. The PV5 supports fast charging also for when Ray needs a boost on the road.

Recent findings suggest that but what about that all-important question of cost? Can we make the bean counters happy? The Kia PV5 retails for AU$56,000 (before on-road costs), which is about the same price as comparable diesel vans like the Ford Transit and the Toyota HiAce. Add to that the savings on fuel, the peace of mind from fuel security, and the reduced servicing and it is easy to build a business case for the Kia PV5 — cost per parcel delivery. The PV5 even comes with vehicle to load.

According to recent reports, and it isn’t made in China! Can the PV5 replace Toyota’s HiAce? Find the answer in this video. The reviewer points out many features that make the PV5 an attractive option: the charge port is on the front. The van has lots of nooks and crannies for storage. She measures storage by capacity to fit in bottles of wine — for example, two in the glove box. There is a step provided to alight the van, aided by grab handles. More storage space is provided above the steering wheel, including a nifty phone slot. There are customizable buttons on the steering wheel to create shortcuts; for example, to the air conditioning settings. A wireless phone charger is nestled near the dash. The glovebox contains the V2L adaptor supplied with the van.

The fact that the van reverts to the lowest regen setting every time you restart the car is a little niggle. That, and there is no frunk — reducing the reviewer’s all-crucial need for wine storage. Full specs can be found here. Kia even gives you helpful advice on how to apply for electric vehicle subsidies (last page, bottom right). One of the pictures that caught my eye shows the PV5 as a flatbed truck.

Recent findings suggest that the PV5 was recently named 2026 International Van of the Year. It measures 4695mm long, 2255mm wide, and 1899mm tall on a 2995mm wheelbase. Range is stated as 416 km, but will of course vary with driving style and load. The battery is a 71.2kWh nickel cobalt manganese (NCM) lithium-ion battery. Kia offers a 165,000 km warranty on the battery. The van is front-wheel drive.

Sources indicate that the PV5 has over 4 cubic metres of cargo capacity, double both that of the ID Buzz and the Tesla Model Y. Space enough for two euro pallets. There are multiple access points, with sliding doors on both sides and barn doors in the rear. The rear barn doors open to 180 degrees, and a low 419mm load height improves accessibility.

Recent findings suggest that goods being shipped are protected by padding on the rear doors and insides of the back. The PV5 can carry up to 740 kg. Tiedowns on the floor of the rear of the van help to secure cargo. There is also a power point in the back of the van. Perhaps a tradie can recharge their tools on site. No frunk for wine.

From the spec sheet: “Standard driver assist features include blind-spot collision avoidance, navigation-based adaptive cruise control, lane-keep assist, lane centring with hands-on detection, and parking collision avoidance assist.”.

A launch in the USA is financially difficult because of the 25% “chicken tax.” Kia builds the PV5 in South Korea and classifies it as a commercial vehicle, and it faces a 25% US import tariff on light trucks and commercial vans.

Sadly, the Kia PV5 doesn’t come in red, but only in white, grey and black. Most companies may take up the option of wrapping the van in their own livery. Overall, we were impressed with Kia PV5 and look forward to seeing more of them on the road throughout the suburbs as Australian delivery drivers move towards a bright electric future.

Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising upcoming approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China.
  • According to recent reports, the findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system.
  • How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising upcoming approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

According to recent reports, the findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis.

It has been revealed that at the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," indicates Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored.".

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis.

The researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

When the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

Industry observers note that this connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

In a recent development, the team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Sources indicate that restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang notes.

Common Supplement Demonstrates Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial.

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

Industry observers note that they conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang indicates. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases.".

Through the newly introduced offering, employers can give access to medications from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk—accompanied by support from licensed professionals, personalized lifestyle coaching, artificial intelligence-enabled food logging and more.

Industry observers note that with each plan year, employers will set a fixed payment per employee per fill that applies consistently across covered medications, the organization mentioned. Employees then pay the remaining balance for each fill. Teladoc manages eligibility, program oversight and consolidated invoicing.

Pharmacy claims are administered on a 100% pass-through basis, including eligibility verification and audit-ready claims documentation.

Moreover, employers can opt in to tie contributions to program engagement, using metrics like food logging and regular weigh-ins, executives say.

The offering is available now, with initial contracted clients slated to launch programs for their employees beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

According to recent reports, “Employers want to provide benefits that help their workforce achieve their health goals and need flexible strategies that work for their organizations,” said Kelly Bliss, Teladoc Health U.S. Group Health president, in a statement. “We are helping employers meet the needs of their employees while providing greater predictability and transparency around healthcare spending. Importantly, we give people a trusted path to high-quality care and affordable access to FDA-approved, authentic medication for meaningful, sustained health outcomes.”.

Alongside the announcement, the company also unveiled upcoming research examining two years of weight-loss outcomes among nearly 23,000 members enrolled in its programs.

Sources indicate that results indicated “clinically meaningful weight loss” increased over time, with 47.7% of members achieving at least 5% weight loss by 24 months. And among those who lost weight during their first year, 53% continued losing additional weight during the second.
