Earlier this year, Optum Rx teased the rollout of newly introduced pharmacy tools designed to address medication cost and access.

Now, the company is offering a look at how those tools work.

It has been revealed that the pharmacy benefit manager said Tuesday that the tools build on Optum's new and more transparent pharmacy model, which the organization confirmed in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. The model moves away from more traditional approaches linked to manufacturer pricing and prescription volume and offers clients a clearly defined fee structure.

The first platform, called Shop MyScript, allows members to compare prices for their medications as well as their options for pharmacies or delivery before the prescription is dispensed. The tool will notify members of potential cost savings shortly after a script is written.

According to recent reports, in addition, Shop MyScript embeds in the prescribing workflow, Optum remarked, so that the member does not have to make comparisons after the fact. If they choose to keep the existing prescription, it will then be sent to the pharmacy.

Optum stated that early adopters have averaged $28 in savings through the program.

"People should have clear information about their medication costs and options when they can actually use it, not after a decision has already been made," said Katte Carey, president of Optum Rx, in the announcement. "These tools give people more information earlier in their journey, so they can make choices that work for them and get the support they need along the way.".

In addition, the pharmacy benefit manager unveiled Optum Assistant, a conversational AI guide that helps members complete routine tasks and track down key information. The tool can triage concerns on a range of topics, from questions about medication and benefits to pharmacy experience challenges.

If the AI guide can't address the individual's needs, they can choose to be connected to live support to find a solution. Optum said about 80% of conversations using the tool led to a resolution without needing a live advocate.

The final upcoming launch aims to support cash-pay options, according to the announcement.

Industry observers note that optum Price Wise will offer members a complete cost breakdown, including the price of a drug and any fees. That total, all-in price allows members to fully understand what their options may be and make the choice that works best for them at the pharmacy counter.

Industry observers note that the PBM stated new tools like these build on Optum's new and more transparent pharmacy model, which the company confirmed in May and shifts to a fee-based structure. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant.
  • Scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an important part of the answer.
  • Recent findings suggest that dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are naturally inclined to avoid. Yet millions of people eventually come to enjoy that same taste, often looking forward to their morning cup. What changes?

Scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an important part of the answer. Their research reveals a little-understood dopamine pathway linking the digestive system and the brain, helping explain how we develop a liking for certain flavors through repeated experience.

Recent findings suggest that dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning. Researchers have long known that it helps the brain recognize experiences worth repeating. However, most studies have examined rapid dopamine signals that appear within seconds of encountering something rewarding, such as the sight of a favorite meal.

The new research, published November 4 in Nature, examines a different system. This slower pathway responds to information coming from inside the body, allowing the brain to learn about the benefits of food after it has been consumed.

"We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," mentioned Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

According to recent reports, the findings offer a possible explanation for why an initially unpleasant flavor can gradually become enjoyable. Once the brain connects the taste of coffee with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better.".

How the Gut Sends Reward Signals to the Brain.

Scientists have spent decades investigating dopamine and its influence on behavior. Its familiar, rapidly acting signals help us respond to opportunities for reward. But dopamine also operates on a slower timescale, through a system that has received far less attention.

According to Knight, this slower process largely unfolds outside our conscious awareness.

When food enters the digestive tract, specialized sensors detect nutrients, including sugar and fat. Information about those nutrients travels toward the brain, where it can produce a dopamine response that develops gradually and continues for several minutes.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate this process, Knight worked with James Grove, PhD, who was a graduate student at the time. They introduced nutrients directly into the stomachs of mice while monitoring dopamine activity throughout their brains.

The researchers used either sugar water or a liquid resembling a milkshake. Delivering these substances directly into the stomach allowed them to separate the effects of nutrients from the experience of tasting food.

The results revealed a powerful, prolonged dopamine response in a specific brain region called the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA.

It has been revealed that the amygdala is involved in emotional processing and learning, including forming associations between experiences and their consequences. Scientists already knew that dopamine was released in this particular region, but its purpose had remained unclear.

"We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role," he said.

Scientists Find a Brain Circuit That Changes Food Preferences.

Finding the dopamine signal was only the beginning. The researchers next wanted to determine whether it actually influenced how animals learned to prefer different flavors.

They first interrupted the newly identified pathway in mice. The animals continued eating normally, indicating that the disruption did not prevent them from consuming food. However, they lost the ability to learn that an unfamiliar flavor was associated with receiving calories.

The team then conducted the opposite experiment.

It has been revealed that after mice tasted a flavor containing no calories, the researchers artificially activated dopamine fibers in the BLA. Remarkably, the animals developed a preference for that flavor even though it provided no nutritional reward.

In effect, stimulating the pathway reproduced the learning signal that nutrients would ordinarily generate.

Together, the experiments highlighted that this dopamine system plays a critical role in teaching the brain which flavors predict rewarding nutritional effects.

A Surprising Discovery in the Left Side of the Brain.

According to recent reports, the researchers also looked for evidence that a comparable process occurs in humans. Brain imaging studies conducted by Knight's collaborators revealed a strikingly similar pattern.

Dana Small, PhD, a psychologist at Yale University, revisited data from an earlier positron emission tomography (PET) study involving 13 men. Participants had consumed either a milkshake or a drink without calories.

Her analysis found that dopamine release following nutrient delivery was especially concentrated in the left side of the BLA.

In a recent development, A separate study led by Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and his colleagues provided additional evidence. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in brain activity associated with blood flow, the researchers examined 38 adults after they consumed glucose, a simple sugar.

They observed increased activity in the same brain region.

One of the most unexpected findings was that the response was not evenly distributed between the brain's two hemispheres.

In both mice and humans, nutrients produced a considerably stronger dopamine response in the left BLA than in the corresponding region on the right.

That imbalance surprised Knight because brain networks responsible for essential functions, such as feeding, are generally expected to work in a relatively symmetrical fashion.

Why the left side plays such a prominent role remains unanswered. Knight's laboratory is now investigating what causes this unusual difference.

Could This Discovery Help Scientists Change Food Cravings?

Recent findings suggest that identifying the pathway provides researchers with a clearer picture of how the digestive system influences the brain's learned responses to food. It also raises an intriguing possibility: Could scientists eventually use this knowledge to change which foods people find appealing?

One area of interest involves GLP-1 medications, a class of drugs that mimic a hormone naturally released by the gut. These medications can substantially alter appetite and eating behavior.

Knight's team did not investigate GLP-1 drugs in the upcoming study, so it remains unknown whether they influence the dopamine pathway the researchers identified.

Still, Knight suggests that one possible explanation for some of their effects could involve reducing the dopamine signals generated when nutrients reach the digestive system. If that happens, foods might gradually become less rewarding because the brain would receive weaker signals reinforcing their flavors.

For now, this remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect of the medications.

The broader implications extend beyond hunger and fullness. Many approaches to changing eating behavior focus on reducing appetite or increasing feelings of satisfaction after a meal. The newly mapped pathway suggests that the brain's process of learning food preferences could eventually become another target.

By influencing how the brain connects flavors with their consequences, future treatments might someday help people develop different preferences rather than simply making them feel less hungry.

"By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods," Knight mentioned.

The discovery offers a latest perspective on why our tastes can change over time. From learning to enjoy bitter coffee to developing a preference for calorie-rich foods, what we love to eat may depend partly on a quiet conversation between the gut and brain that continues long after the first bite.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-DK106399, R01-DK138127, R01-NS116626, and R01-DK145100 and F31-NS120468).

Medicare Shared Savings Program saved $2.5B last year: CMS" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Medicare Shared Savings Program has reached the highest savings number in its history, according to latest federal data.

Sources indicate that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said Tuesday that the program generated more than $2.5 billion in net savings for Medicare in 2025, making for the ninth year in a row that it led to cost savings. The agency added that every accountable care organization met or exceeded quality reporting requirements.

ACOs participating in MSSP earned $4.9 billion in shared savings payments during 2025, CMS stated, with 80% of organizations earning performance payments.

As of 2026, 511 ACOs representing more than 700,000 providers are participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, which represents 12.6 million people enrolled in traditional Medicare, another record.

It has been revealed that "Patients want doctors who work together, care that puts their needs first, and fewer unnecessary hurdles—that is what accountable care is designed to deliver," said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These record savings show the power of rewarding providers for quality and coordination. We want more people with Medicare, and more of the providers who care for them, to benefit from this approach.".

Sources indicate that CMS stated that it wants to make it easier for providers to participate in MSSP if they choose, especially given the program's results to date. It included changes in the latest Physician Fee Schedule to encourage participation, including increased opportunity for certain ACOs to earn shared savings and new financial incentives to draw in first-time participants.

It has been revealed that in addition, CMS remarked that would create more predictable spending targets that make planning and participation straightforward. The agency is also aiming to streamline patient notices and simplify required technology.

“We are excited to see continued progress on both savings and enrollment for Medicare beneficiaries. Beneficiaries are best served when a provider is watching out for them and coordinating their care,” said Center for Medicare Director John Brooks in the announcement.

Emily Brower, CEO of the National Association of ACOs, mentioned in a statement that the 2025 results "build on years of progress and underscore what the accountable care community can accomplish through collaboration, innovation and the widespread adoption of proven best practices.".

"NAACOS looks forward to partnering with CMS to build on this momentum," remarked Brower. "Policies that unleash innovation, reduce burden, and create sustainability through fair and predictable budgets will allow ACOs to deliver even greater value for patients and the Medicare program.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Sources indicate that scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.

In a recent development, the research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

"Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo indicates. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms.".

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss.

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an important question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The fresh findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

According to recent reports, "This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman states. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body.".

It has been revealed that the peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Sources indicate that guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery.

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a organization co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce important interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

It has been revealed that the scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

It has been revealed that the results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance.

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

Industry observers note that when the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

These measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

"You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman notes. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection.".

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

However, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially key new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research.

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he notes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 11:38 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

The neocloud boom is entering a sorting phase, and global cloud availability is emerging as the line between providers built for enterprise AI and those built to rent out racks of graphics processing units.

In a recent development, with agentic AI moving from pilots into production, buyers are looking past raw GPU counts toward integrated platforms they can build on. That shift is redrawing the competitive map for cloud AI infrastructure. Enterprise practitioners are now starting ambitious agentic AI agendas, and they need the full stack of services behind AI-native applications rather than standalone clusters, according to Kevin Cochrane (pictured, right), chief marketing officer of Vultr.

Recent findings suggest that “There are those providers that are trusted platforms, that are global cloud platforms that have the totality of services that are required for real agentic AI deployments,” Cochrane stated. “We’ll continue to see a separation of the pack and there’ll be those that are trusted platforms that enterprises can rely on and there’ll be those that aren’t.”.

Cochrane and Duncan Ng (left), vice president of solutions engineering at Vultr, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why agentic AI is reviving demand for central processing units, how Vultr builds data centers as integrated systems and which neocloud providers are likely to survive consolidation. (* Disclosure below.).

According to recent reports, calling a service an enterprise cloud takes more than racking accelerators. Vultr organizes its footprint into data center regions, each of which can control multiple facilities on one network. Developers get one application programming interface they can hook into a Terraform template, Cochrane explained. Many rivals, by contrast, stood up individual sites rapidly to serve bespoke customer contracts.

Recent findings suggest that “In traditional neoclouds, the data centers are actually islands. They’re not connected. It’s not one unified global network. It’s not one unified global platform,” Cochrane noted. “These are like individual data centers stood up very promptly for bespoke customer contract. That is not a platform.”.

Recent findings suggest that agentic AI is also reshaping the hardware mix inside those regions. Reasoning models now let agents chain dozens of steps, call tools and validate results in flight — work that leans heavily on CPUs, according to Ng. Vultr ran a cloud for more than a decade before the GPU rush and has used processors from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. as the backbone of its CPU fleet for several years, he added. The tech giant has since extended that partnership to accelerators with a $1.2 billion order for AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems.

“This increased density, this increased usage — these are just new hosting companies,” Ng said. “This is just a new application that is 10 times more compute dense than the last that we’re trying to sell to.”.

Enterprises are finally moving those workloads out of pilot and into production, Ng noted. One Significant Four global systems integrator uses Vultr as the substrate for a risk management service. Vultr has been rolling out platform upgrades aimed at enterprise agentic AI to support that kind of deployment.

“What they’re doing is something that used to take consulting hours, people poring through spreadsheets and poring through invoices, poring through declarations,” he said. “They now are able to automate significant portions of this to serve a larger number of their customers and do a deeper dive into their risk supply chains.”.

Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination pulled by White House" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The White House pulled the nomination for Heidi Overton, M.D., Ph.D., to lead the FDA just hours before the Senate was scheduled to vote on her confirmation.

The move hardly comes as a surprise after Overton’s confirmation hearing before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee drew contention.

In a recent development, the news was first reported by Axios on Tuesday evening. The White House confirmed the news to Fierce the following morning.

In September, the HELP committee questioned Overton in a hearing marked by tightrope-walking on issues like vaccines, abortions, flavored vapes and whether or not President Donald Trump is capable of being wrong.

In a recent development, overton conceded multiple times during the hearing that vaccines approved by the FDA, as well as the “abortion pill” mifepristone, are safe and effective. But she stopped short of admitting that Trump has been wrong when dispensing medical information out of line with what scientific evidence indicates.

Overton’s nomination faced mounting pushback and uncertainty from senators ahead of a planned HELP Committee vote on Nov. 18. Fierce reached out to Sen. Ed Markey, the veteran Democratic lawmaker from Massachusetts, ahead of the vote, and he told Fierce that he would “vote against her nomination, and I urge my colleagues to do the same.”.

“The FDA needs a leader who will stand up for science and for our kids’ safety, not one who stood by while both were undermined,” he added.

In a recent development, republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who chairs the Senate health committee, and other Republicans had also raised questions about Overton's nomination.

As support for Overton looked thin, Republicans were discussing Sen. Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, as a potential replacement, Semafor reported today. Health Secretary Kennedy reportedly met with Marshall in recent days to discuss filling the role, according to Politico, but the White House told the publication that it is not considering him.

Industry observers note that robert Steinbrook, M.D., health research group director for Public Citizen, commented today urging the HELP committee to reject Overton’s nomination: “The FDA needs a strong commissioner who stands for science and the integrity of the agency,” Steinbrook mentioned. “Overton is the wrong choice for FDA Commissioner and has done nothing to dispel the well-founded reasons to oppose her candidacy.”.

Analysts from Citi shared that the White House’s decision to pull the nomination has a negative impact on biopharma, “extending uncertainty around permanent agency leadership.”.

“We view the withdrawal as a modest sentiment negative, but not a material near-term change to the regulatory environment facing most drug and biologics sponsors,” the analysts said in the note.

The withdrawal of Overton's nomination leaves a gap at an FDA that has already faced significant upheaval. The White House only shifted its focus to Overton in August, after the agency had spent three months without a permanent leader.

Since former FDA commissioner Marty Makary, M.D., departed the agency in May, Kyle Diamantas, who hails from the agency’s food regulation division, has been at the helm in an interim capacity.

Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A surprising fresh study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight.
  • Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide crucial clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A surprising fresh study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops.

Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide crucial clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition.

The results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival.

It has been revealed that "Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an notable question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," said corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center.

Obesity Linked to Up to 27% Lower Risk of Death.

It has been revealed that the researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics.

According to recent reports, people classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight.

"This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," noted Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author.

Tracking Weight and Dementia Over 24 Years.

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.

The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.

Because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward.

This extended timeline was especially vital because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider.

Could Weight Loss Explain the Dementia Paradox?

One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent.

Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.

According to recent reports, this creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated.

Another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group.

To determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality.

Why Extra Weight Might Help People With Dementia.

Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia.

In a recent development, one possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease.

Dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health.

"Nutrition can be a big problem for people with dementia," said Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves.".

Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences.

The researchers emphasize that important questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia.

Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

#18904. Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1612 w)

Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered new clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels.
  • Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death.
  • According to recent reports, reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered new clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels. Their findings point to biological processes involving other fat-carrying particles in the blood that may contribute to cardiovascular damage in ways that go beyond cholesterol buildup. By identifying these previously poorly understood mechanisms, the research could help pave the way for more targeted strategies to prevent heart disease and potentially save lives.

Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes responsible for more than 80% of those deaths. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits containing cholesterol (cholesterol) build up inside the arteries that supply blood to the heart. If left untreated, the condition can eventually cause a heart attack.

According to recent reports, reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack. However, bringing LDL cholesterol into the recommended range does not eliminate the danger. Some patients continue to develop coronary heart disease despite successful treatment, suggesting that other particles transporting fats through the bloodstream play an crucial role. Until recently, the biological reasons behind this remaining risk were not well understood.

"For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs," indicates Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology, in Sweden.

According to recent reports, cholesterol is a substance similar to fat that circulates in the bloodstream. The body needs it to build cells and manufacture certain vitamins and hormones. Problems can arise when too much cholesterol accumulates in blood vessel walls, creating deposits called plaques.

These plaques can narrow arteries and interfere with blood flow. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot may form quickly and completely obstruct the affected vessel, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Because cholesterol and other fats cannot travel through the blood on their own, they are transported by specialized particles known as lipoproteins. Three major classes of these particles contain a surface protein called apolipoprotein B (apoB). When too many of these particles circulate in the blood, they can deliver excess cholesterol into artery walls. The cholesterol they carry is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol.".

Sources indicate that to investigate these unanswered questions, the scientists used proteomics analysis to examine how three types of fat-carrying particles (LDL, TRL and Lp(a)) affect the body and may contribute to heart disease. This approach allowed the team to investigate biological changes associated with the particles rather than focusing exclusively on the cholesterol they carry.

Recent findings suggest that all three types can contribute to cholesterol deposits inside artery walls, although LDL, which stands for low-density lipoprotein, is the most common. In a previous study, the same research group found that counting harmful lipoprotein particles was the most effective way to predict future heart disease risk.

According to recent reports, the researchers also identified two particularly vital contributors beyond LDL: triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, or TRL, and lipoprotein(a), known as Lp(a). Their earlier findings suggested that each of these particles poses a greater risk individually than an LDL particle. As a result, TRL and Lp(a) are considered major contributors to the cardiovascular danger that can persist even after LDL cholesterol has been successfully reduced.

Proteomics is the systematic, large-scale examination and measurement of proteins within cells, tissues, or body fluids at a particular point in time.

While genomics investigates a person's relatively stable DNA, proteomics focuses on proteins, which are constantly responding to changes inside the body. These molecules help construct tissues, process food, transmit hormonal messages, and defend against infections.

Because protein patterns shift in response to factors such as diet, stress, aging, and disease, analyzing them can provide a snapshot of current biological activity. Proteomics can help researchers identify biomarkers, diagnose medical conditions, and track how patients respond to treatment.

Blood Proteins Reveal Hidden Heart Disease Risks.

The upcoming investigation focused on proteins, which perform countless essential functions throughout the body. Unlike genetic information, which remains largely unchanged, protein levels and activity can respond to diet, stress, aging, and illness. Studying these changes can therefore provide valuable insights into the body's current biological condition.

Recent findings suggest that researchers analyzed measurements of nearly 3,000 proteins found in blood samples and compared the results with genetic information and long-term health records. This combination helped them identify protein patterns associated with different lipoprotein particles and provided clues about how those particles might contribute to damage inside the arteries.

Sources indicate that one of the most striking discoveries involved TRL and Lp(a). Although these are distinct types of particles, their associated blood protein patterns demonstrated substantial similarities. Those overlapping patterns also appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease.

The researchers found that these particles carried proteins capable of attracting immune cells, potentially encouraging inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. This suggests that TRL and Lp(a) may contribute to cardiovascular disease through some of the same biological processes, rather than simply depositing cholesterol in the arteries.

In a recent development, LDL highlighted a different pattern. Its associated proteins were primarily connected to cholesterol accumulation in artery walls, highlighting an vital distinction between the ways these three types of particles may contribute to heart disease.

"The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings," indicates Morze. "It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future.".

How LDL, TRL, and Lp(a) Affect Heart Health.

The three types of lipoproteins examined in the study, LDL, TRL, and Lp(a), transport different amounts of cholesterol and other fats through the bloodstream. Each contains the structural protein apolipoprotein B, or apoB.

It has been revealed that all three can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty material accumulates inside blood vessel walls. As these deposits develop, they increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

In a recent development, LDL: Low-density lipoprotein transports most of the cholesterol circulating in the blood. An LDL cholesterol measurement indicates how much cholesterol is contained within these particles.

Recent findings suggest that TRL: Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins transport cholesterol along with triglycerides, which the body uses as an important energy source. As triglycerides are removed from these particles, the remaining fragments can deposit cholesterol inside artery walls. In this study, the TRL measurements primarily reflected liver-produced particles called VLDL and the remnants they leave behind.

Recent findings suggest that lp(a): Lipoprotein(a) resembles an LDL particle but contains an additional protein known as apolipoprotein(a). Higher levels of Lp(a) are already recognized as an established risk factor for coronary heart disease.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Disease Prevention?

In a recent development, by identifying biological pathways associated with cardiovascular risk beyond LDL cholesterol, the findings offer researchers latest possibilities for developing more personalized prevention strategies. In particular, the shared inflammatory and blood vessel effects linked to TRL and Lp(a) could become promising areas for further investigation.

However, the research did not evaluate a new treatment or establish a blood protein test ready for routine clinical use. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether measuring these biological processes, or developing treatments that target them, can improve protection against heart disease.

"Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention," states Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. "Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments.".

Industry observers note that the results reinforce the importance of controlling LDL cholesterol while revealing why cholesterol reduction alone may not address every source of cardiovascular risk. Understanding the additional ways blood particles affect arteries could ultimately help scientists develop more precise approaches to protecting heart health.

Study Details and Research Institutions.

The study, "Apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins: distinct roles in atherosclerosis revealed by plasma proteomic profiling," was published in the European Heart Journal.

The research authors are Jakub Morze, Elias Björnson, Michael Y Mi, Martin Adiels, Giorgio E Melloni, Gonçalo Rosas da Silva, Andrzej Rynkiewicz, Nicholas A Marston, Marta Guasch-Ferré, Michael Y Tsai, Jerome I Rotter, Robert E Gerszten, Qi Sun, Frank B Hu, Rikard Landberg, Göran Bergström, Chris J Packard, Jan Borén and Clemens Wittenbecher.

At the time of the research, the authors were affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology and the Institute of Medicine at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Harvard Medical School, USA; AstraZeneca, Sweden; Municipal Hospital in Olsztyn, Poland; University of Copenhagen, Denmark; University of Minnesota, USA; The Lundquist Institute at Harbour-UCLA Medical Center in Torrance, USA; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, USA; and the University of Glasgow, UK.

Materials provided by Chalmers University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

HLTH 2026: How Whoop aims to play a bigger role in healthcare

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fiercehealthcare

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LAS VEGAS—Whoop gained traction as a performance wearable used by elite athletes, professional teams and Olympians to track physiological strain and sleep.
  • In a recent development, the firm has evolved into a broader clinical and digital health platform that layers medical-grade hardware, blood diagnostics, electronic health record (EHR) syncing, and physician care on top of its continuous biometric tracking.
  • It has been revealed that whoop is a screenless, wrist-worn device that measures strain, recovery and sleep 24/7, paired with Whoop Coach, an AI-powered, in-app health and fitness assistant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: How Whoop aims to play a bigger role in healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Whoop gained traction as a performance wearable used by elite athletes, professional teams and Olympians to track physiological strain and sleep.

In a recent development, the firm has evolved into a broader clinical and digital health platform that layers medical-grade hardware, blood diagnostics, electronic health record (EHR) syncing, and physician care on top of its continuous biometric tracking. The company's FDA-cleared ECG detects signs of atrial fibrillation and allows members to share results with their healthcare provider.

It has been revealed that whoop is a screenless, wrist-worn device that measures strain, recovery and sleep 24/7, paired with Whoop Coach, an AI-powered, in-app health and fitness assistant. The company expanded its Advanced Labs testing—combining Quest blood testing, clinician reviews and AI insights—to non-members, alongside integrating Grail's multi-cancer early detection test. Whoop partners with health platform HealthEx to let customers connect their medical records directly to the Whoop app, combining medical history with biometric data. A feature rolled out earlier this year lets Whoop members directly connect with clinicians through the app, including live, on-demand video consultations.

Industry observers note that the tech giant has raised over $900 million to date, including a $575 million series G round in March, pushing its valuation to $10 billion. Whoop told Bloomberg it aims to hire 600 people this year, a roughly 75% boost to its headcount, as it works to further integrate AI into its health and wellness monitoring tools and to expand internationally. The company is on track for an initial public offering in 18 months, executives told Bloomberg in August.

The company is positioning itself as a continuous health monitor that goes beyond fitness tracking. The device's 24/7 physiological data can function almost like an ongoing health check, becoming a bridge between everyday health and medical care, Will Ahmed, founder and CEO of Whoop, stated during an on-stage interview at HLTH on Tuesday.

Ahmed argued that the conventional annual medical physical is "frozen in time.".

Sources indicate that "The reality is wearing a continuous health monitor like Whoop that should be a 24/7 annual checkup. That's how it should function from a data standpoint," he said during a fireside chat with Michael Phelps, U.S. former competitive swimmer, who is the most decorated Olympian in history with 23 gold medals, and also a Whoop customer since 2015.

Recent findings suggest that "Then there will be alerts when something is really wrong, and particularly as we combine these different data sources together, again, 24/7 physiological data, blood tests, medical records, how you're feeling and contextual cues. When we have all this information in one place, and now we've got 3.5 million members, about to be 4 million members, it's just amazing the insights that you can pull together from that. And so you can start to predict that someone may need to get a cancer screening, or may actually have a real heart problem," he remarked.

Whoop can pull together biometric data, labs, medical records and information to establish a baseline for an individual, recognize meaningful changes and recommend an action. By combining continuous monitoring with information such as blood tests, the company hopes to help consumers piece together health signals and determine when they may need care, Ahmed mentioned.

For Phelps, Whoop has shifted from being about maximizing elite athletic performance to helping him manage his health, energy and recovery around everyday life and longevity, he told the audience.

Industry observers note that "For me, for 20-plus years, I've been trying to chase time, and now I'm just trying to be the healthiest person that I can be," Phelps noted. "For me, the data that I get every single day, if my body isn't 100% or I'm not full go, then I take a step back and I tone down my workout. When I'm talking to my trainer, I'm taking it down a little bit, so I have enough energy and I have what I need to be a good dad, to be a good husband, to be a good worker, hard worker, whatever it is, just to be a good person.".

Whoop sees opportunities to turn deviations from an individual's baseline into actionable signals. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Phelps said his Whoop device signaled that his temperature, respiratory rate and HRV changed, but he noted that the real benefit was that Whoop knew what normal looked like for him.

Using biometric data to recognize signals in a person's health can have broader implications, Ahmed noted, citing examples where members identified potentially serious health problems after noticing significant changes in their physiological data.

According to recent reports, "We're just starting to see all of these different maps presenting themselves, and it's very empowering. We're excited about the role that we can play with the broader health ecosystem," Ahmed remarked.

Ahmed said Whoop's high user engagement and continuous monitoring can fill gaps between doctors' visits and provide clinically relevant information to care teams.

"I do believe that technology like Whoop can make the whole system much more efficient and also make a doctor's life easier if we do our jobs properly, which is again to say, how do you take all this information that's being collected about a patient or a consumer and how do you simplify it to the one, two, or three questions that a doctor might actually want to know the answer to before you show up to their office?" he said.

Ahmed sees the AI coach evolving into a personal health companion sitting on top of a longitudinal health record.

According to recent reports, "That's another area that we're really excited about, where this idea that you can have a conversation with Whoop or what feels like this entity that sits on top of your data, and all of a sudden you feel like you have a health companion, and yes, you've got 24/7 physiological data from sensors, but you can also now have your medical records. You can also now have your blood tests. There are all sorts of conversational cues. 'How are you feeling today?' 'Did you drink alcohol last night?' Were you traveling?' You put all that information together, all that data in one place, and the insights are quite profound," he said.

Partnerships with other digital health companies and acquisitions help Whoop broaden the platform, he noted.

"We like to think about it from the consumer's vantage point first, which is to say, if you're an individual, if you're a consumer, what is data that you want on your body or you need on your body, and that may be data that's being collected somewhere else, in which case, we feel like there could be an opportunity for a partnership," Ahmed said, adding, "We're also comfortable now acquiring technology and acquiring different innovations, which has become more of a muscle that we've built over the last 12 months.".

Whoop believes its biggest strategic advantage is the consumer relationship.

Members open the app roughly eight times a day and wear the device nearly 23 hours a day.

"There are so many of us who have been in health tech where we would die for that kind of engagement, and I think that's something we're always striving for because we're an industry that was never built with the consumer in the center," noted Lynne O'Keefe, founder and manager partner of Define Ventures, who moderated the on-stage interview.

It has been revealed that the company is strategically expanding into an older, more medical population. Whoop is a participant in the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' ACCESS model. Ahmed remarked members 65 and older are actually Whoop's most highly engaged demographic, challenging the assumption that consumer health technology primarily appeals to younger people.

According to recent reports, "It's clearly a population that cares a lot about their health. They want to focus on what's going on with their blood pressure, their ECG, or whether they need to send data to their doctors," he noted.

Ahmed framed CMS' ACCESS model as a move from consumers simply paying for a wearable toward government reimbursement tied to measurable health outcomes, such as improvements in blood pressure or weight.

Sources indicate that "I think as a model of innovation for a government and its citizens, it's pretty interesting because it incentivizes companies to actually create technology or programs that are making people healthier. It should change the cost curve because you're paying if that outcome is delivered, and then to the consumer, you're both hopefully being healthier and not paying for a product that otherwise would have had to," he said.

Whoop also positions itself as a platform that can wrap around drugs and other healthcare interventions. The firm unveiled this week a partnership with Novo Nordisk as part of the pharma company's redesign of its direct-to-consumer NovoCare program. Novo Nordisk relaunched its NovoCare direct-to-consumer program. Patients taking a GLP-1 can integrate wearable data from Whoop as part of their program.

Whoop can function as a potential companion for GLP-1 owners, monitoring exercise, sleep, resting heart rate, HRV and other signals while helping users preserve health and fitness during treatment, Ahmed said.

In a recent development, when asked about the future vision for Whoop, he mentioned, "I think in simple terms, it's our responsibility to build technology that either makes you healthier or one day saves your life. You're going to have all of this health data on your body. I think organizing that information in one place, alongside 24/7 wearable data, and alongside a powerful AI that can sit on top of that data and go off on your behalf and take actions and schedule appointments with the doctor, or go speak to your doctor on your behalf, or alert you when something's wrong," he said.

It has been revealed that he added, "God forbid this day comes, but you should wake up and be told from Whoop you need to go to the doctor in the next 30 minutes, and it's been scheduled, and you show up, and all of a sudden you find out that you're having a heart attack, or you're having some serious life event. To me, that feels like an inevitable future, and I do predict that a large percentage of humanity in the future will be wearing a continuous health monitor.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

Recent findings suggest that in recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Industry observers note that not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

Recent findings suggest that with digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

Sources indicate that the approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

In a recent development, REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

In a recent development, if you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech manufacturer could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

According to recent reports, investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chinese biotech robotics firm MegaRobo Co.
  • Founded in 2016, MegaRobo builds robotic systems that let artificial intelligence software run physical experiments, alongside precision measurement and inspection tools for manufacturers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 11:45 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Chinese biotech robotics firm MegaRobo Co. Ltd. today announced it has raised $200 million in new funding to invest in its core technology and expand its automated life sciences infrastructure for increasingly complex physical systems.

Founded in 2016, MegaRobo builds robotic systems that let artificial intelligence software run physical experiments, alongside precision measurement and inspection tools for manufacturers.

Sources indicate that investors joining the round included Oman Investment Authority, Asia Investment Capital, Granite Asia, Sinovation Ventures and CMB International. The company raised $600 million to date across multiple funding rounds, including nearly $300 million in Series C during 2022.

Industry observers note that “The first generation of AI learned from humanity’s accumulated knowledge. The next generation will increasingly learn by acting in the physical world — through experiments, production and continuous feedback,” said founder and Chief Executive Daniel Huang. “That shift changes AI from a system that interprets the world into one that can help create upcoming knowledge, materials, processes and products.”.

In a recent development, the manufacturer’s two most prominently marketed offerings are Megalaxy Lab, an AI-connected experimental platform and CellVue T2000, its automated cell-imaging instrument. Both appear on the company’s English-language homepage. MegaRobo also sells more specialized lab equipment, including the Auflo sample-preparation workstation and the Seloris cell culturing automation system.

The key distinction is that Megalaxy Lab is the public face for the company’s AI-for-science strategy, while CellVue and other systems represent concrete examples of the instruments it builds for the industry.

In a recent development, the organization stated through Megalaxy it is making real-world experimentation programmable and accessible. Researchers and AI agents can configure experiments, route them through automated laboratory systems, track execution, receive structured, machine-readable results, and feed them directly into the next cycle of scientific reasoning. This includes virtual large data readouts that can be amplified as digital twins representing the scientific data, protein design, biochemistry and other properties.

MegaRobo said it’s working together with industry partners, including Tencent Cloud and Twist Bioscience, to expand its capability in the AI Science community with the launch of Poreva Open, a global AI protein design challenge open to all models and technical approaches. Megalaxy will provide wet-lab validation for more than 10,000 protein design sequences, creating an opportunity to test models against real experimental data.

It has been revealed that the company is also developing the One Intelligence Stack as a common technology foundation for instruments, machines, materials processes and real-world feedback. #18899. Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1417 w)
